topic_summaries.UK Heatwave, Drought and Wildfire Emerge:
• Guardian, Independent, Metro and GB News all cover the Cobra emergency meeting, but Guardian/Independent frame it as a national crisis requiring ministerial leadership, while Metro focuses on procedural detail
• Guardian and Independent emphasise climate change accountability and policy failure; GB News highlights economic consequences (food security, wine industry) with notably lighter framing
• Evening Standard stands out with visual/satellite imagery approach to London's drought impact, while Channel 4 News focuses on meteorological records and wildfire risk statistics
topic_summaries.Global Climate Records and Extreme Weath:
• The Guardian and The Independent lead coverage with record-breaking heat data — US July records, Western European temperature highs, and ocean heat — while Channel 4 News frames the same crisis through cumulative climate statistics (38 years of glacier melt, rising sea levels)

• The Guardian broadens scope beyond temperature records to cascading consequences: drought (Lake Mead, Danube wrecks, water rationing), wildfires (Canada, Indonesia), and economic/policy dimensions (India's green growth, fossil fuel profits); The Independent adds nuclear energy vulnerability and endangered species rollbacks

• Daily Mail covers wildfire air pollution and a damning 2025 climate report but buries both behind unrelated clickbait headlines, suggesting lower editorial prioritisation of the climate story
topic_summaries.UK Net Zero and Green Energy Policy:
• GB News dominates coverage with a sceptical, cost-focused framing — portraying Net Zero targets as damaging to workers, industry and living standards; The Independent and BBC take a more neutral or policy-descriptive approach
• GB News and The i both cover potential EV mandate rollbacks, but The i warns of consumer price rises while GB News frames relaxation as Labour "finally" admitting green "lunacy"
• Metro and Evening Standard highlight local community pushback against specific green infrastructure projects (Greenlink interconnector, Scottish wind farm), focusing on environmental and heritage concerns rather than broader policy debate
topic_summaries.North Sea Oil and Gas Debate:
• GB News frames Jackdaw approval as urgent common sense, emphasising energy supply benefits (1.4m homes heated); The Guardian and Channel 4 News foreground climate risk and political accountability
• The Guardian focuses on political pressure on Andy Burnham as a key decision-maker; Channel 4 News amplifies climate expert voices opposing new extraction
• GB News uses adversarial language ("end the madness") favouring industry; The Guardian and Channel 4 News adopt a more cautious, climate-concerned tone
topic_summaries.Record Ocean Temperatures and El Niño:
• BBC and Daily Mail both lead with the record 20.96°C ocean temperature figure, but BBC frames it scientifically while Daily Mail uses alarming "Super El Niño" language
• The Guardian and The Independent focus on downstream consequences — flooding in the western US and Atlantic hurricane patterns respectively — rather than the temperature record itself
• The Independent uniquely highlights humanitarian impact, citing the UN's warning of 49 million more people facing acute hunger
topic_summaries.Water Pollution and Environmental Standa:
• Metro, The i, and Channel 4 News all cover the Environment Agency's damning water quality findings, but Metro leads with beach sickness reports and Surfers Against Sewage, while The i and Channel 4 News foreground the statistical scale (14% good ecological health, zero in good chemical health)

• The Guardian's two articles sit apart from the main water pollution story, covering foraging and plastics in food waste schemes — tangentially environmental but not engaging with the EA findings at all
topic_summaries.AI and Technology's Environmental Impact:
• The Guardian dominates coverage, framing AI's environmental impact through local human consequences (water/energy competition in Slough) and systemic climate harm (fossil fuel enablement outweighing AI's green benefits)

• The Independent focuses on a specific corporate accountability angle, highlighting Amazon's Texas plant as a potential record-breaking polluter despite net-zero pledges

• Sky News and other outlets offer little usable content on this topic, leaving The Guardian as the primary voice shaping the AI-environment narrative in this sample

articles.jina_text:
Prime minister Andy Burnham will chair a meeting of the government's Cobra emergency committee this afternoon in response to the heat, the wildfires it has fuelled and the drought now covering much of the country.
It is the second Cobra meeting on the heat this year, after one held during the June heatwave. Temperatures are forecast to reach 33C today and up to 38C tomorrow.
A Downing Street spokesperson said the government understood that firefighters, farmers and NHS staff were all facing pressures connected to the weather.





On Tuesday a firefighter union chief warned the country faces a “national emergency” amid ongoing wildfires.
Southern Water is pushing for a rare drought order which would ban the filling of non-domestic swimming pools.
The firm said an “exceptional” shortage of rain in the South East “demonstrates a clear threat to supplies” in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. 165,000 people in the Southampton West supply area could “soon be significantly affected” by a restricted water supply, it added.


Thames Water said that thousands of homes and businesses have now been left without water or with low pressure after pipes burst in London and Essex.

articles.jina_text:
Swimming pools and car washes are among the UK businesses that could be hit by a water ban as providers look to conserve resources amid drought conditions and an upcoming fifth heatwave.
Southern Water has applied to the government for permission to issue a “non-essential use ban” in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. If granted and put into action, the policy would prevent businesses from activities like washing cars with hosepipes and filling private swimming pools.
It comes as almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been plunged into drought.


Temperatures are set to soar to as high as 38C this week as parts of the country face their fifth heatwave this summer.





A Southern Water spokesperson confirmed it had applied for a drought order and a non-essential use ban as a precaution, but that it does not currently plan to enact the measures.

Andy Burnham to chair emergency Cobra meeting amid extreme heat


High temperatures continue across UK with 38C forecast on Thursday and wildfires stretching emergency services




Andy Burnham will chair an emergency Cobra meeting in response to extreme heat, which has caused wildfires and plunged many parts of Britain into drought.
The prime minister will meet ministers, officials and agencies on Wednesday as high temperatures continue across the UK, with temperatures of 33C forecast and up to 38C on Thursday.

A No 10 spokesperson said the government understood firefighters, farmers and NHS staff were all facing challenges connected to the weather.
It will be the second Cobra meeting this year on heatwaves, after one took place amid high temperatures in June. It comes as parts of the country face their fifth heatwave this summer and the number of days reaching 30C in any year in the UK hits a new record, with 35 days so far beating the 34 days set in 1995, according to the Met Office.


The climate breakdown has been linked to the increasing frequency of wildfires, burning larger areas, across many parts of the world. The “fire wave” under way in the UK is the most widespread the country has ever experienced, with the combination of wet winters and prolonged heatwaves exacerbating the risk.

“We know how challenging this summer is proving, particularly for firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units.
“We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies and safeguard the environment.”
Ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the Home Office and Department of Health and Social Care, as well as officials from the Environment Agency, will attend the Cobra meeting.

The news that we have spent £1bn just to turn off excess wind farm capacity so far this year – and that this number is only going to grow – certainly implies that it’s the wind farms that are in danger of bankrupting UK PLC. Down with this sort of thing. 
Actually, though, that £1bn bill stems not from the fact wind power is bad but because it’s too good. According to The Times, “most of the cost comes from paying gas-fired power plants to fire up to cover for wind turbines that have to be turned off because of” – here comes the kicker – “insufficient cabling capacity”. As more wind power has come on stream, more capacity to transport it to actual people hasn’t. That, thanks to Britain’s esoteric energy market, means we’re now paying renewable energy suppliers in rural areas to switch off (so as not to overload the network), and fossil fuels nearer actual people to switch on (because we still need the power). And the more turbines we have, the more that bill will go up. Oops. 
These figures come from the Wasted Wind website supported by Octopus Energy, which is currently lobbying the government to end this madness by replacing national energy pricing with a more regional scheme. For those without such skin in the game, though, this mess provides proof of a much simpler thesis: that Britain has lost the ability to build the infrastructure it needs to function.

 
When you go looking for evidence for this problem, you start seeing it everywhere (or rather, you don’t, because nobody’s built it). The largest, most expensive and highest profile mess is HS2, which as originally conceived would have connected almost every major British city and, by adding capacity and removing bottlenecks, benefited smaller places far off the route, too. 
After spiralling costs and repeated cutbacks, alas, it will instead serve mainly to create a third mainline route between London and Birmingham and not a lot else. The reasons for this have more to do with political chaos and over-scoping in a doomed attempt to assuage Nimbys than with the project itself, but nonetheless, this is not a lot to show for a bill of £100bn+. It’s all a little embarrassing for the nation that invented the railways. 

London’s Hammersmith Bridge closed to motor traffic due to structural problems in 2019 (Photo: Richard Baker/Getty) 
That’s just the start. Since the passage of the Leeds Supertram Act in 1993, the largest city in Western Europe without a fixed transport system has laid not an inch of track. (France, in that time, has managed to build 22 different networks.) A third runway at Heathrow was first proposed in 2009. All-British chocolate bar made by scientists using Reading-grown cocoa


Master’s student made first bar with 100% UK ingredients since 1932 to highlight effect of climate crisis on cocoa plants




The late queen was the only person in history to have ever eaten a chocolate bar made with 100% British ingredients, after she was given one as a six-year-old in 1932 by the confectioner Rowntree’s.
The bar was created from a glasshouse-grown cocoa plant, at Rowntree’s headquarters in York.

But now, others could have the same experience after scientists at the University of Reading created a bar with cocoa beans grown in Berkshire.


Raw cacao beans are coated in a white flesh ‘that tastes like lychee’. Photograph: University of Reading
The bar was crafted to celebrate the university’s 100th anniversary, made with cocoa grown from plants in the institute’s collection.


The UK makes some of the world’s best chocolate in a market worth £10.4bn, but the industry is entirely reliant on imported cocoa.
Maha Khan, a master’s student at the university, decided to make a bar with cocoa from Reading. She harvested, fermented, and processed the beans at the university’s food department.







Why hot weather and chocolate can go together

Read more
She said: “It has been amazing to follow the entire chocolate-making process, from pod to bean to bar, without leaving Reading.
“This British bar of chocolate highlights the precarious nature of our food supplies. Cocoa plants are very sensitive to changes in temperature and rainfall, and climate change is already causing problems in countries that produce most of the world’s cocoa. Protecting different varieties is vital if farmers need hardier plants that can cope with a changing climate.
“I hope this shows people just how much work goes into the chocolate we enjoy, and how important it is to protect cocoa farmers and communities around the world.”
She said the chocolate is “delicious”, adding that it had a very rich flavour: “It’s incredible to taste the complexity of the flavour profiles as the cocoa is made from plants originating from over 300 varieties grown here. It was also really interesting to taste the raw cacao before it gets processed – the beans are coated in a white flesh that tastes like lychee and isn’t something many people in this country get to try.”

articles.raw_content:
Consumers could see an end to “heavy” discounts on electric vehicles (EVs) as ministers look to water down net-zero targets, according to car industry experts.



Under current laws, 80 per cent of all new cars sold in the UK must be electric by 2030 under the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, rising from 33 per cent from 2026. 



It is understood that ministers are set to launch a consultation in the coming days on loosening these rules, with numbers ranging from 50 per cent to 70 per cent under consideration. 





The European Commission has already modified its plans to ban the sale of petrol and diesel vehicles by 2035, shifting the requirement for a 100 per cent ban on internal combustion engines to a 90 per cent zero-emissions target.



Good deals on electric cars

articles.jina_text:
July was just the hottest month on record in the contiguous U.S., according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration - and shows little signs of slowing down for August. 
Fortunately, it appears temperatures will drop for many areas this week - but much of the southern U.S. will see dangerous heat before the end of August.
“Potentially record-breaking heat will grip the Southeast to south-central U.S. into next week, with heat indices reaching 105–115 degrees Fahrenheit and little nighttime relief,” NOAA’s National Weather Service warned. 





August is typically not quite as hot as July, but meteorologists say the record sets up August for more extreme events. Some local records have already been broken. 
“Wow - Pueblo just set its all-time hottest August temperature on record. 107 degrees at the Pueblo Airport so far,” Colorado meteorologist Chris Bianchi wrote on Bluesky. “That's also just two degrees shy of the all-time hottest temp there.”

That’s between 0.1-0.2 degrees warmer than the previous records set in July 2012 and July 1936, during the Dust Bowl.
Interestingly, daytime temperatures were only the sixth warmest. That meant America just wasn’t cooling down at night, NOAA explained.



“Daytime maximum temperatures averaged 89.5 degrees Fahrenheit, 2.9 degrees Fahrenheit above average, ranking as the sixth-warmest month on record for average high temperatures, while overnight minimum temperatures averaged 64.2 degrees Fahrenheit, 3.7 degrees Fahrenheit above average,” NOAA explained, “ranking as the warmest month on record for average low temperatures, surpassing July 2022 by 0.7 degrees Fahrenheit.”

The Guardian view on wildfires: firefighters can’t handle this crisis alone

Editorial





The response to this summer’s record heat and drought should be led by ministers – not left to the emergency services





The wildfire that began on protected heathland in the New Forest in Hampshire on Sunday was reported to be under control on Tuesday. But with temperatures forecast to reach 36C or higher in parts of England on Thursday, the risk of further outbreaks remains high. Firefighters responded to 185 wildfires in the first 10 days of August. In coastal Suffolk, conservationists and locals are counting the cost of the blaze that devastated Dunwich Heath. Its vegetation and rare bird populations are expected to take decades to recover.
Although the immediate cause of many wildfires is litter, the risks are elevated by heat and drought, and repeated warnings from climate scientists do not necessarily lessen the shock and distress caused. As people and governments across Europe assess this summer’s damage, experts including the UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, hope that the fires will focus minds on the urgent necessity of cutting emissions – as well as investing in emergency planning. Europe is currently heating up faster than any other continent, due in part to proximity to the melting Arctic.



The global, existential nature of the climate crisis makes it an awkward fit with Andy Burnham’s current focus on “everyday fixes”. But if he does not find more to say about the summer’s disasters, he is in danger of being left behind. The National Trust has already surpassed its £500,000 fundraising target to restore Dunwich Heath. Conservationists and farmers are publicly debating the best ways to prevent fires. The Fire Brigades Union (FBU) is pushing for 5,000 additional firefighters across the UK, along with new equipment.


View image in fullscreen
Hilary McGrady, the National Trust director general. Photograph: Shutterstock
In March, the then fire safety minister, Samantha Dixon, said that the fire and rescue service had suffered from “decades of drift and inertia”. Her speech also confirmed that a new College of Fire and Rescue would oversee professional standards, as recommended by the Grenfell inquiry. But three weeks ago Ms Dixon was sacked. Samuel Alito gained up to $2.9m from oil and gas assets since joining supreme court, analysis shows


Critics argue US high court justice should recuse himself from upcoming fossil fuel firms’ climate accountability case




The supreme court justice Samuel Alito gained up to $2.9m from his fossil fuel interests between 2005 and 2024, a new review of financial disclosures shows.
The analysis from the non-profit advocacy group and judicial watchdog Court Accountability, shared exclusively with the Guardian, found that even at the lowest range of estimates, Alito gained almost $400,000 from his oil and gas interests since being tapped for the high court by George W Bush in 2005.

The findings come as the supreme court prepares to take up a case in which the oil companies Suncor Energy and Exxon asked the justices to find that federal law prevents subnational governments from filing lawsuits against fossil fuel producers for the climate-warming effects of their products.


The supreme court said this month it will hear oral arguments in the case on 5 October, the opening day of its new term. The Trump administration, which is siding with the oil companies, has asked for 10 minutes of argument time. Court Accountability and other groups have called for a Senate committee to investigate Alito, the sole supreme court justice with holdings in energy companies, and said he should recuse himself.
He and the court rejected those calls.
Supreme court ethics rules focus specifically on investments in companies named in court cases. In May, a supreme court spokesperson told NBC News that Alito was not required to recuse himself from the Suncor lawsuit as his holdings do not include the companies directly named in the case, Suncor and ExxonMobil.
But Lisa Graves, co-founder of Court Accountability who authored the new analysis, said Alito’s oil-tied wealth provides grounds to question whether Alito can impartially weigh in on cases affecting the entire fossil fuel sector.
“You might have real appreciation for how that industry has helped make it possible for you to perhaps buy a second home on the water, or live a [certain] lifestyle,” she said.


The Guardian has contacted the supreme court and Alito for comment.
Mineral rights
Alito’s financial disclosures show his reported assets – excluding his home and other personal property – grew from about $1.1m in 2005 to between $3.4m and $8.4m by 2024. Federal financial disclosures report assets in broad value ranges.

The National Trust for Scotland says it objects to plans by ScottishPower Renewables to build a two gigawatt wind farm near Colonsay and Islay.

        







The National Trust for Scotland has raised concerns about the impact the proposed wind farm could have on bird populations on islands it owns (Owen Humphreys/PA)


Katrine Bussey
4 minutes ago





News Briefings

Sign up

A planned wind farm could have a “significant” impact on some island communities, conservation chiefs at the National Trust for Scotland (NTS) have warned.




The charity has set out details of its opposition to the proposed MachairWind development, which would see 91 to 144 turbines sited in waters to the north-west of Islay and to the west of Colonsay on Scotland’s west coast.








Developer ScottishPower Renewables has said the project could generate around two gigawatts (GW) of electricity – enough to power the equivalent of up to two million homes.




If it gets the go ahead from the Scottish Government, the energy firm said the wind farm could be up and running by 2033.




However the NTS has raised concerns about the impact the development could have on some of the island communities it cares for.




A statement from the charity made clear it “supports the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy, including the development of offshore wind”, but it added that such projects “must be at the right scale and in the right location to minimise negative impacts on communities, heritage, and nature”.


The proposal could see up to 144 turbines sited between Islay and Colonsay (PA)
PA Wire




It added: “The trust does not agree that the MachairWind offshore wind farm is in the right location.












“The scale and magnitude of impact will be significant on island communities, landscape, marine mammals and environment, the tourist economy, habitability, and the cultural heritage of Iona, Staffa, and the Treshnish Isles, locations that are in the care of the trust.”




The NTS owns much of Iona, which is famous for sacred sites such as Iona Abbey, while Staffa, a national nature reserve also owned by the conservation charity, is famed for its puffin population and Fingal’s Cave.








The Treshnish Isles, which are owned by the NTS, have been designated as a site of special scientific interest (SSI) and are said to be an important nesting site for puffins, guillemots, and razorbills.




The NTS said it is “concerned about the ornithological impact of the MachairWind development”, suggesting this should be “closely examined” when considering if the project goes ahead.

articles.title: Don’t despair about what’s happening to our planet. That’s what they want you to feel
articles.raw_rss: There are social tipping points when the seemingly impossible suddenly becomes inevitable. Good journalism plays an essential role in helping drive these shifts and shows us how real change can happenClimate campaign 2026: help us reach 20,000 acts of supportThere are many reasons to despair: our green and pleasant land is parched and brown, reservoirs are depleted, and wildfires are racking the UK, Europe and the US. There are social tipping points when the seemingly impossible suddenly becomes inevitable. Good journalism plays an essential role in helping drive these shifts and shows us how real change can happen 
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 20,000 acts of support 





There are many reasons to despair: our green and pleasant land is parched and brown, reservoirs are depleted, and wildfires are racking the UK, Europe and the US. But there are many more reasons not to despair: despair is self-fulfilling; despair is disempowering; despair is what the bastards want you to feel. But above all, despair is irrational. Let me explain why.
However sophisticated our forecasting tools may be, we simply have no means of knowing what comes next. Like the climate, like every ecosystem, society is a complex system. Its properties and adaptive responses cannot be predicted by studying its components in isolation, regardless of the brilliance of social scientists and futurologists. Things happen - unexpected things - sometimes at astonishing speed. In other words, society has tipping points. It can quickly flip from one equilibrium state to another.



Take Ireland, to give just one example. Until a few decades ago, the Republic of Ireland was a Catholic theocracy. It had been that way since the 1920s. If anything, for most of the 20th century, the Catholic church seemed to tighten its grip. Breaking that grip was almost unimaginable. But then a number of events combined in unexpected ways. A series of appalling scandals came to light: systematic sexual violence, the kidnapping of women and children, slave labour and mass mortality in church institutions. Travel and mass media allowed Irish people to see what social and sexual liberation looked like in other countries. The media and international forums allowed brave activists, whose voices had long been suppressed, to be heard more widely. The walls fell faster than anyone could have guessed. Before long, equal marriage and the right to abortion were both legally sanctioned: a shift that had been almost unimaginable.
The same can be said for the collapse of state communism, and the end of just about every empire and monarchy that once looked unassailable. The fossil fuel empire is not exempt.
The complex system we call society has two equilibrium states: impossible and inevitable. The change we want always looks impossible. Votes for women? You must be off your rocker. Independence for India? Britain will never let it go. Civil rights? Ridiculous! But with sustained pressure, a bit of luck, a change in circumstance, bang!, the impossible happens. Then everyone says, “Well, that was inevitable, wasn’t it?”


I think we could be approaching a tipping point on climate breakdown. For years we’ve been told, “You’re asking for the moon. Fossil fuels are here to stay.” Part of me has believed it. AI’s potential climate benefits outweighed by role in boosting fossil fuels, study finds


Modelling finds AI-driven productivity gains in coal, oil and gas enable more emissions than applications in renewables avoid




AI-driven productivity gains enable more planet-heating pollution from fossil fuels than they avoid from renewables, a study has found.
Researchers modelled the technical potential for AI to boost clean power generation along with projections for how it can help produce coal, oil and gas. Across 64 scenarios, they found net yearly carbon pollution rose by 0.47-1.8 gigatonnes, or about 1-5% of the energy sector’s annual emissions.

The study is the first to quantify the climate impact of AI across the full power sector. Previous research has explored its indirect climate benefits – such as reducing renewable downtime and optimising electricity grids – while ignoring the extra pollution from increasing productivity in drilling oil wells and extracting gas.
“What most studies have done so far … is compare the datacentre energy use with the emissions savings AI has,” said Lynn Kaack, an assistant professor of computer science and public policy at the Hertie School who provided feedback on a draft of the research. “They completely omit this picture of AI causing increases in emissions.”


View image in fullscreen
A solar array installed in a river in Bangladesh. Photograph: Bipul Ahmed/NurPhoto/Shutterstock
The researchers found net emissions only fell in scenarios where AI did not increase productivity in the fossil fuel sector. If clean and dirty energy facilities were to adopt AI at similar rates, they found, the productivity gains for renewables would have to outpace those for fossil fuels by at least four times for emissions to break even.


Holly Alpine, a co-author of the study and a former Microsoft employee who left to co-found the Enabled Emissions campaign group, said the research team used a conservative assumption that AI adoption would happen at the same rate for fossil fuels and renewables.
“Fossil fuel applications are already happening at scale today – real contracts, real deployment, with evidence from industry operators and financial analysts,” she said. “Renewables applications are still largely at the pilot or academic-study stage – more speculative, more dependent on deployment barriers like permitting and interconnection getting resolved.”

articles.jina_text:
As we mentioned in the opening post, amber heat health alerts come into force across most of England from 9am today and will last until 9am on Friday.
As well as a rise in deaths and likely “significant” impacts across health and social care services, here are some of the other risks associated with the amber category, as outlined by the UK Health Security Agency:
 
 
internal temperatures in hospitals and care homes may exceed the recommended threshold for clinical risk assessment 
 
the heat affecting the ability of the workforce to deliver services 
 
indoor environments overheating increasing the risk to some vulnerable people 
 
issues managing medicines 
 
increased demand for power exceeding capacity 
 
possible travel delays 
 
water‑related incidents may increase, including risks from cold‑water shock and drowning 

Health alerts are set to come into force across England this morning as parts of the UK brace for fifth climate crisis-driven heatwave this summer.
Amber heat health alerts have been issued for all regions in England, except the north-east, which mean significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures, according to the UK’s Health Security Agency (UKHSA). The alerts stretch from 9am on Tuesday until 9am on Friday.
The north-east will be under a yellow health alert, which is less intense than the amber category but is still linked to a rise in deaths, particularly among those aged 65 and over or with health conditions, and a likely increase in demand for health services.


View image in fullscreen
An aerial view shows the dried and cracked bed of the depleted Hollow Pond and Leyton flats near Wanstead, east London, on 10 August 2026. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty Images
The alerts come a day after four more regions of England were officially declared to be in drought: the East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs.
They joined seven English regions, alongside the whole of Wales, already under drought status since last month: East Anglia, Hertfordshire and London, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the West Midlands, and Wessex (covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire and south Gloucestershire).
The Environment Agency said 71.3% of England is experiencing “flash drought”, as a dry start to August followed the country’s driest July on record.
On Tuesday, highs of 29C in Cardiff, 28C in Manchester and 25C in London are forecast before temperatures soar to the mid-30s in some areas on Thursday, according to the Met Office, with temperatures possibly exceeding 36C in some places.

articles.jina_text:
With a spell of heatwaves and record-breaking temperatures, chances are you’re considering long-term cooling suggestions – rather than a quick fix such as portable air conditioning units.
Indeed, Simon Bones, a leading sustainability expert and founder of intelligent retrofit company Genous, helping homeowners retrofit their homes for a greener future, says there’s been renewed interest… particularly this summer.
“Dramatically so… either for air conditioning on its own (which we actually don’t do), or in combination with other kinds of renewables, where people are thinking about things like heat pumps.





“They’re increasingly asking, ‘can it cool too?’. So I would say it’s been dramatically different from what we would be getting any other time of year.”





open image in gallery
(Alamy/PA)
In answer to the question, Bones says some heat pumps can cool, if configured correctly. “It can get quite complicated, but you’ve got various options.”

Incorporating renewables
When it comes to electricity-consuming items such as fans or air-conditioning, Bones says these can be effective, but use a lot of power.


As an alternative, he suggests installing an air-to-water heat pump with underfloor heating which provides mild cooling by flowing cooler water through the heating circuits.
Moreover, he says any cooling takes a lot of energy, so integrating with solar panels is smart. “Generating electricity from solar panels, storing it and then reusing it from home batteries to heat your home from a heat pump.”





open image in gallery
(Alamy/PA)
“And because you can buy it, store it, use it at a different time and generate it yourself, it means you’ve got more control over it. And it’s much lower carbon because heat pumps in particular, are four times plus more efficient than even the best gas or oil boiler.



“And solar panels as well,” he adds. “They don’t consume anything apart from sunlight, so they’re fully green once they’re in.”





Bones also suggests thinking about cooling as part of a holistic renewable strategy. “It’s really about the financial,” he highlights. “Running air conditioning, they’re powerful units and reasonably expensive.
“And if you’re thinking about using solar panels, they generate power more when it’s hot and sunny, and therefore you’re aligning your production with your demand.”





open image in gallery
(Alamy/PA)
He says they also deflect some of the heat from the roof as a side-benefit, “but on a day like today, the sun is shining and people have air conditioning”.

articles.jina_text:
The Royal Parks, Kew and Chiswick House and Gardens are among the capital's popular outdoor amenities already hit by increasingly extreme weather caused by climate change, according to the National Lottery Heritage Fund and Historic England report. 








They warn green spaces are already being affected by paths and drainage systems not fit for current conditions, trees lost to drought and high winds, and potential loss of entire groups of plants to diseases affecting box, ash, sweet chestnut and oak.




The report says historic parks and gardens across the UK employ more than 32,000 people and contribute £2.9billion to the UK economy each year from international visitors alone.




But they are increasingly vulnerable to damage from harsher, more widespread drought, intense rainfall, more severe storms and pests which can thrive in warmer conditions.




The warning was sounded as heat health alerts come into force at the start of the fifth heatwave of the year, with almost three-quarters of England now in drought.













From 9am on Tuesday, heat health alerts issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) are in place across England until Friday evening.


A walker protects themselves from the sun on the scorched grass of Hyde Park on August 9
AFP/Getty




Highs of 32C and 35C are expected in London on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the Met Office.




Amber heat health alerts have been issued for most of England including the South East. 




The Environment Agency (EA) said 71.3% of England is experiencing “flash drought”, as a dry start to August followed the country’s driest July on record.









The National Lottery Heritage Fund and Historic England report, which drew on interviews, surveys and analysis, found many park and garden managers are unprepared for the severe impacts of climate change – with staff wanting increased advice and guidance and warning a lack of funding is stopping them implementing changes.




And while all sites are responding in practical ways where they can, for example prioritising actions that will help adapt to climate change, they warn they are spending more time on emergency responses and maintenance.

In today’s newsletter: As we enter our fifth summer heatwave, Andy Burnham’s government is looking at what the UK should do with its remaining North Sea oil and gasGood morning. What a difference a new job can make. “To have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can’t have any new oil or gasfields … It’s irresponsible and shortsighted to be funding new #fossilfuels when we need to be getting to #NetZero.”

 This was the 2022 message from Miatta Fahnbulleh, now the secretary of state for energy security and net zero. It’s a testament to her remarkable rise that Fahnbulleh wasn’t even an MP when she posted it four years ago. Today, she is in the cabinet, facing (or is the face of, at least) one of the most challenging, and potentially controversial questions looming for the new government: to drill or not to drill, baby?
Two sites are the focus of fierce debate. Yesterday, a public consultation on whether to greenlight extraction at one of them – Jackdaw – closed. As we enter yet another heatwave, what his government does next will be a defining signal of intent on the issue.

articles.jina_text:
Firefighters in the UK are under increased pressure as a result of an “unprecedented summer of dangerous and volatile wildfires”, the Fire Brigades Union has said, as many parts of the country brace for a fifth heatwave of the year.
As authorities declared almost three-quarters of England was now in drought, Steve Wright, the FBU general secretary, said the unpredictable environmental challenges the UK was now confronted with meant it was a “national priority” to have enough properly equipped firefighters to “face these threats”.

More than 120 firefighters continued to tackle a blaze in the New Forest national park in Hampshire that began on Sunday. Nottinghamshire fire and rescue service declared a major incident on Sunday as two large fires in woodland near Mansfield put a significant strain on resources there.



Emergency calls to the London fire brigade have increased by almost a third this summer as firefighters have battled a surge in wildfires and flooding in the capital, according to an internal briefing seen by the Guardian.
The document warned that the brigade had come under mounting pressure from extreme weather and predicted the trend would continue because of the climate crisis. Between 1 April and 9 July, the service received 75,652 emergency calls – 31% more than the previous five-year average – while the number of incidents rose by nearly a quarter to 42,943.
London firefighters responded to 392 wildfires during the period, alongside 68 water rescues, the briefing said, as repeated spells of hot weather and heavy thunderstorms stretched the service’s resources.
The climate breakdown has been linked to the increasing frequency of wildfires, burning larger areas, across many parts of the world. The so-called “fire wave” under way in the UK is the most widespread the country has ever seen, with the combination of wet winters and prolonged heatwaves exacerbating the risk.
In recent weeks, there have been large blazes in places including Dunwich Heath in Suffolk, Headon Warren on the Isle of Wight, Llanwonno in the Rhondda valley in south Wales, and the Cairngorms national park in Scotland.


The National Drought Group, which met on Monday, said 71.3% of England was now experiencing a “flash drought”, which develops very quickly brought about by a combination of very low rainfall and higher temperatures. About 45 million people live in a drought area and more than 27 million are now living under water use restrictions.
The group said all regions of the country were experiencing pressure on their water resources, with growing pressure on agriculture, public supplies, navigation and the environment.

View image in fullscreen

July was hottest month ever recorded in US as heatwaves scorched country


Scientists have made clear that the elevated heat in the US was being amplified by the human-caused climate crisis




July was the hottest month ever recorded in the US, with repeated, scorching heatwaves across much of the country helping shatter all previous monthly temperature records stretching back over the full 132 years of reliable measurements.
Last month’s average temperature was 3.3F (1.8C) higher than the 20th century average for the contiguous United States, which excludes Alaska and Hawaii, according to new data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).

This means the month was the hottest July, and hottest of all months, in records that go back to 1895. It surpasses previous high marks set in July 1936, in the teeth of Dust Bowl conditions, and July 2012.

In July, the US blistered under three separate heat dome events, where soaring temperatures where held in place over a region by slow-moving high pressure weather systems. Extreme heat hit much of the US west, the Rockies, upper midwest, the Gulf of Mexico coast and south-east, according to Noaa. Wyoming recorded its hottest ever July amid temperatures a huge 5.1F above average.


Parts of the US spent the month blanketed under a haze of wildfire smoke, with large blazes engulfing forests in Canada and the US’s Pacific north-west. Scientists have made clear that the elevated heat, along with vast fires, was being significantly amplified by the human-caused climate crisis, accelerated by the burning of fossil fuels.
Heat-trapping gases released by the combustion of coal, oil and gas are driving up global temperatures and fueling deadly heatwaves that have this year roiled the US and Europe, which is having its hottest summer on record. Sprawling forest fires, resulting in the evacuations of hundreds of thousands of people and the inhalation of toxic smoke for millions more, have become a feature of the season in North America and Europe.
The average monthly heat record set in July – although the record for maximum daily temperatures remains July 2024 – has taken a toll on the lives of many Americans, polling released by AP-NORC last week showed.
Nearly half of people in the US said the impact on their electricity bills, which have risen even as people have sought to cool themselves with air conditioning, has been “major”. Meanwhile, about 40% of people said the heat had altered their travel plans.

articles.raw_rss: More areas of England have been moved into drought status as the country faces another heatwave.
articles.raw_meta: Temperatures remain high in the capital, with the mercury tipped to reach 35C on Thursday
articles.jina_text:
More than two thirds of England is in drought as a dry start to August follows the country’s driest July on record, according to the Environment Agency (EA).




It comes as the UKHSA issues amber heat health alerts for London and the South East from 9am on Tuesday until 9pm on Friday.








Temperatures remain high in the capital, with the mercury tipped to reach 35C on Thursday.




The Met Office is reportedly considering issuing a rare red health alert as hot conditions remain.




On Monday, the East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs became the latest areas to move into drought.


The dried-out Brockwell Park in south London
PA




The announcement came after a meeting of officials, water companies and farming leaders under the National Drought Group, which warned that all regions of the country are experiencing pressure on their water resources, with impacts on agriculture, public water supplies and the environment.




Last week, the EA announced that half of England had plunged into flash drought – one which develops very quickly because of a combination of very low rainfall and high temperatures – and the latest announcement means 71.3 per cent of the country is in drought.




The North East and Yorkshire have moved to “prolonged dry weather” status, the stage before drought, and nowhere in England is in “normal” status, the EA said.











The latest drought warnings came as parts of the UK braced for the fifth heatwave of the summer, with temperatures expected to climb into the mid 30Cs later in the week.




This summer has been one of extreme heat and dry conditions, with two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June that led to the deaths of more than 2,800 people, followed by further heatwaves in July.









England had its driest July since records began in 1836, with some areas experiencing no rain for the entire month




In the latest heat spike, amber heat health alerts have been issued for most of England, with officials urging people to take simple steps to stay safe, such as drinking plenty of water, checking on vulnerable friends and family, and avoiding the sun at the hottest part of the day.


The dried and cracked bed of the depleted Hollow Pond and Leyton flats near Wanstead, east London
AFP/Getty Images




The UK is increasingly struggling with the impact of more extreme weather such as drought, heatwaves and wildfires fuelled by climate change, which is mostly caused by burning fossil fuels in power plants, in vehicles, to heat homes and for industry.

‘It’s very challenging’: how the Duke of Westminster’s farm is taking on the climate crisis


Amid world pressure from heatwaves and fertiliser shortages, billionaire’s business has invested in circular farming and biomethane




There is a distinctive smell of cow manure in the air at the Duke of Westminster’s dairy farm near Chester. It is a world away from the collection of grand West End properties controlled by the duke that form the backbone of his near £10bn fortune, a decade on from becoming Britain’s youngest billionaire.
As part of his 349-year-old Grosvenor empire, Lea Manor Farm on the duke’s Eaton Estate in north-west England has fared better than most dairy farms in recent years.

But it has also been hit by declining milk prices and other challenges faced by British farmers. A series of heatwaves causing drought, with a fifth looming this week – combined with fertiliser shortages triggered by the Iran war, diseases and a scarcity of workers since Brexit – have made farming very difficult.


Milk prices are cyclical; higher farm-gate prices in the UK last year encouraged an expansion of production, and oversupply in the UK and overseas has led to price reductions of up to 50% this year, according to Mark Roach, the managing director of Grosvenor Farms. “I can’t imagine any other industries suffering a 50% reduction.”
Lea Manor has been an arable and livestock farm for centuries, with a focus on potatoes between 1984 and 2002, when it switched to cows after the realisation that growing potatoes on the heavy Cheshire clay was not sustainable.
The farm at Eaton Estate, which is part of Grosvenor’s sprawling portfolio of offices, shops, homes, woods and farmland, has 77 staff and 2,600 Holstein friesian cows; it produces more than 34m litres of milk a year – 13,200 litres a cow – and supplies Müller and Tesco. It is surrounded by fields where animal feed such as wheat, maize, barley and rye is grown, set in 4,685 hectares (11,577 acres) of land.


View image in fullscreen
Mark Roach, the managing director of Grosvenor Farms, says oversupply has led to price reductions of up to 50% this year. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian


This year’s heatwaves – supercharged by the escalating climate crisis – have piled more pressure on farmers. When temperatures rise above 25C, cows become more lethargic, eat less and produce less milk. At 36C during the June heatwave, each Grosvenor cow produced up to six litres less milk a day, with the heat partly mitigated by a sprinkler system and the large airy barns.

Can Florida’s ‘coastal corridor’ project safeguard wildlife and boost economy?


Conservationists have created a ‘coastal corridor’ of ocean-based projects designed to preserve and nourish vulnerable marine life




From disappearing manatees to bleached coral reefs, gender-changing turtles and oyster beds destroyed by hurricanes, no other state’s marine life faces the magnitude of climate-related challenges that Florida’s does.
Now, wildlife authorities are attempting to bring some cohesion to tackling the diverse slate of issues by borrowing from a playbook that has already proved successful on land.

The Florida fish and wildlife conservation commission (FWC), and its charitable arm, the Fish and Wildlife Foundation of Florida (FWFF), have announced the creation of an ambitious “coastal corridor”, an interconnected chain of ocean-based projects and enhancements designed to preserve and nourish vulnerable marine creatures.


It replicates to a significant degree the state’s wildlife corridor, an 18m-acre (7m-hectare) project established in 2021 to provide a safe, contiguous habitat spanning much of Florida where rare or threatened land-based species including birds, reptiles, panthers and bears can flourish.
Featuring projects including habitat restoration, fisheries enhancement and improved public access and coastal resilience along Florida’s Atlantic and Gulf coasts, the project aims to create a connected network of artificial reefs, oyster beds, seagrass and mangroves on which marine life can thrive.
“The goal is to protect and connect all these important habitats for fish and wildlife,” said Nick Wiley, the former head of FWC who was appointed in April as executive director of FWFF.
“Everyone has seen how successful the wildlife corridor initiative has been, rallying everybody around the mission. The wildlife species needed these travel lanes and corridors across the state, but it also highlighted how private landowners contribute to federal, state and county public lands and how all that fits together.
“Our board members were really inspired by that, looking at our coast, our fisheries and the coastal communities, and from the beaches, estuaries, all the way out into the deeper water.”
The coastal corridor is designed to not only protect Florida’s precious marine legacy, but also the economic riches of its waters. Recreational fishing alone brings in $14bn a year, and provides 120,000 jobs, the foundation said. Another $3.1bn and 39,000 jobs come from creating and maintaining artificial reefs.

articles.raw_rss: Global oceans recorded their hottest July on record, partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions, as wildfires continue to ravage western Europe.

articles.jina_text:
The world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific, according to the EU's climate monitoring service.
The average sea surface temperature (SST) outside the world's polar regions - between 60 degrees north and 60 degrees south - was 20.96C last month, beating the previous high of 20.89C, set in 2023.
Last month was the joint second-warmest July globally on record, with temperatures 1.47C above the estimated pre-industrial average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.
Meanwhile, Western Europe experienced its hottest ever June and July, with prolonged hot and dry conditions fuelling extreme wildfires across the region.
Elsewhere, the UK is braced for its fifth heatwave of the year this week, as persistent dry weather puts further pressure on water supplies and could see more areas officially declared in drought.






What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures?





11 June


Rhine falls to record low levels as drought strains Europe's rivers





3 August




Around Europe, sea surface temperatures in July reached record highs along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, contributing to widespread strong and severe marine heatwaves.
Sea temperatures remained exceptionally high across much of the tropical Pacific, where El Niño conditions are developing and forecast to strengthen in the coming months. 
El Niño is a natural weather pattern in the Pacific that combined with human-driven global warming can cause temperature spikes and more extreme weather.
Oceans are a vital regulator of the climate, absorbing most of the excess heat generated by greenhouse gas emissions and producing half of Earth's oxygen.
The greatest effect of ocean warming is on sea level rise. As seawater warms it expands, and this thermal expansion accounts for roughly a third of sea level rise recorded by scientists to date. That water encroaches on low-lying coasts and island nations.
Hotter seas are also driving longer and fiercer marine heatwaves, which have bleached coral reefs on a mass scale and decimated kelp forests and fisheries.
Warmer ocean surfaces also evaporate more heat and moisture into the air, intensifying tropical storms and loading them with heavier rainfall.

articles.title: Drought expected to be declared in more parts of England
articles.raw_rss: Officials will meet on Monday to assess water shortages across the country as a new heatwave builds.
articles.raw_meta: Officials will meet on Monday to assess water shortages across the country as a new heatwave builds.
articles.jina_text:
A drought is expected to be declared in more parts of England on Monday, joining half of the country and the whole of Wales.
The National Drought Group – made up of regulators, government officials, water companies and agricultural bodies - will meet on Monday afternoon to assess the situation across England.
Almost all of southern England is already officially in drought after an exceptionally hot and dry summer, with heatwave conditions set to return for many this week.
Liz Bentley, chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, said the number of people under a hosepipe ban is likely to increase from the 23 million already experiencing restrictions.
She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the country had experienced an "exceptional, unprecedented summer", which was becoming the "new norm".
Bentley predicted north-west England, which is already classed as being under a less severe "prolonged dry weather" status, would be among those areas where drought could be declared on Monday.
The areas already officially in drought are East Anglia, Hertfordshire, London, Thames Valley, Hampshire, the Isle of Wight, Devon, Cornwall, the West Midlands and Wessex (Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire, and south Gloucestershire).


Much of England is already classified as being in drought, with several areas in a less severe 'prolonged dry weather' status














There is no single definition of drought, but it usually refers to a period of prolonged unusually dry weather that can have impacts on people, nature and the environment.
Last month, England and Wales saw the driest July since records began in 1836 - while for southern England, it was the driest month ever recorded.
River levels have continued to fall after less than 10mm of rain across England for the seventh consecutive week.
The Environment Agency has warned that low water levels have resulted in potential navigation issues for boats on the Thames, Lark and Ouse.
Reservoir levels have also continued to decline, with almost all across England below normal and five classed as "exceptionally low", according to the agency.
The National Farmers Union (NFU) has warned that continued dry weather could lead to some food shortages.
NFU president Tom Bradshaw said yields of wheat and oats were "very, very poor" this year and warned livestock farmers have had to use their winter feed rations because they have been unable to grow grass.
The week ahead is forecast to remain mostly dry, with temperatures soaring across much of England and Wales.





Temperatures will peak on Thursday before dropping slightly over the weekend - and for England and Wales, there is no significant rainfall expected in the foreseeable future.

Western Europe has set a new average temperature record for the June/July period set in 2022, according to the European climate agency Copernicus.
The extreme heat began in May and has contributed to major wildfires, prolonged drought and thousands of projected heat-related deaths.
Globally, 2026 has been the third-hottest year, behind 2024 and 2025, climate statistics show. But there is still time to catch up. 





Thanks to the one-two punch of accelerated human-caused global warming and a supersized El Niño, a periodic warming of parts of the Pacific that leads to temperature variations around the globe, there’s an increasing chance that by the end of the year, 2026 could become the hottest year on record, beating out 2024 — or at least come close, scientists said.
Last month saw the highest average sea surface temperature ever recorded for July across the extra-polar oceans, or the oceans free of seasonal sea ice, Copernicus said.

Indonesia on Monday escalated efforts to combat a surge of wildfires across the archipelago, deploying hundreds of firefighters and disaster personnel as well as helicopters. 
Blazes, exacerbated by an unusually dry season, are ravaging a popular national park in East Java and peatlands in Sumatra.
The most extensive fire is consuming the Mount Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in the province of East Java where more than 740 hectares lie scorched. 





The forestry ministry said on Sunday that dry weather and intensifying El Nino conditions had heightened the risk of further forest and land fires during the peak dry season. 
The ministry said large areas of dry grassland, vegetation and protected edelweiss flowers had been destroyed, with flames spreading to the Penanjakan area, a renowned viewpoint for tourists visiting Mount Bromo. No injuries or evacuations were reported.

articles.title: The UK’s cleanest beaches revealed after hundreds fall ill swimming in British waters
articles.raw_content:
New research has revealed the cleanest beaches across the UK (Picture: Getty Images/iStockphoto)



Britain’s polluted waters have been back in the spotlight since the Environment Agency revealed that that almost all of England’s lakes, rivers and coastal waters are heaving with toxic chemicals. Charming.

And now the water crisis is deepening after Surfers Against Sewage (SAS) received a record number of sickness reports from beachgoers.

Jo Morley, SAS’s head of campaigns, accused water companies of ‘making us sick’ after decades of pumping sewage into open waters.

The affected beaches include several Blue Flag spots, which are given their title for the highest water quality, biodiversity levels and safety.

So where can we swim in peace? 

New research from the Foundation for Environmental Education has identified the beaches with the cleanest waters across the UK.


	
			
		Saltdean Beach is known for its rock pools (Picture: Getty Images)



There are 63 in England and nine in Northern Ireland, including high profile locations such as Hastings, Saltdean, Sandbanks, and Blackpool Sands.

Hastings beach hugs the length of the town, from the fishing quarter and the Old Town in the east, past the amusement arcades and the pier, towards the Marina and onto St Leonard-on-Sea.

Regular cleaning efforts are organised by volunteers from Plastic Free Hastings, as well as routine maintenance carried out by Hastings Council and a service for reporting litter.

Writing on TripAdviso

articles.title: I hiked Cambodia’s highest mountain and stumbled across a plane crash
articles.raw_content:
My guide said to me: There is something special we want to show you.’ (Picture: Supplied)



While millions of visitors head to Cambodia each year for the temples of Angkor Wat, thanks to my odd obsession for climbing the highest mountains in every country I visit, I found myself hiking through dense jungle instead.

Having hired a local guide from a nearby village, we’d set off into thick rainforest where there were no crowds, no souvenir stalls and barely another person in sight.

We were in search of the country’s highest peak, Mount Aural, a little-known summit rising more than 1,800 metres above sea level in the remote Cardamom Mountains.

For hours we followed little more than a faint trail winding through humid jungle, broken only by small metal altitude markers nailed to trees. My guide, Pu Makara, spoke almost no English, so our conversations were relayed over walkie-talkie by another guide, Lina Seanglay, who had been forced to remain at base camp after falling ill.

After five hours and covering 15km, we finally reached the summit. I had assumed that once we caught our breath, we would head back to the basecamp where we started out. 


	
			
		Sadie was taken on a detour through the thick, dense jungle (Picture: Supplied)





But then Lina asked over the radio whether I’d like to take a different route back down. ‘There is something special I want Pu Makara to show you,’ she said with an air of mystery.

The guide wasn’t exaggerating.

While millions of visitors head to Cambodia each year for the temples of Angkor Wat, thanks to my odd obsession for climbing the highest mountains in every country I visit, I found myself hiking through dense jungle instead. 
Having hired a local guide from a nearby village, we’d set off into thick rainforest where there were no crowds, no souvenir stalls and barely another person in sight. 
We were in search of the country’s highest peak, Mount Aural, a little-known summit rising more than 1,800 metres above sea level in the remote Cardamom Mountains. 
For hours we followed little more than a faint trail winding through humid jungle, broken only by small metal altitude markers nailed to trees. My guide, Pu Makara, spoke almost no English, so our conversations were relayed over walkie-talkie by another guide, Lina Seanglay, who had been forced to remain at base camp after falling ill. 

 

After five hours and covering 15km, we finally reached the summit. I had assumed that once we caught our breath, we would head back to the basecamp where we started out.  
 
   
Sadie was taken on a detour through the thick, dense jungle (Picture: Supplied)  
But then Lina asked over the radio whether I’d like to take a different route back down. ‘There is something special I want Pu Makara to show you,’ she said with an air of mystery. 

 
The guide wasn’t exaggerating. After taking a detour through dense forest, an enormous aircraft suddenly emerged from the trees. 
Wedged between giant boulders, the military transport plane appeared almost frozen in time. Moss and lichen had slowly swallowed parts of its aluminium shell, while vines wrapped around broken wings that had remained untouched for decades. 
It felt less like stumbling across a tourist attraction and more like discovering a forgotten piece of history. For 30 minutes we took in the sight of this mysterious wreck, being careful not to trip on the undergrowth enveloping the steep mountain edge. 
Pu Makara gestured to ask if I wanted a photo beside it, but it didn’t seem appropriate. In my mind, it stood as a memorial to those who lost their lives on that fateful flight, so instead I paused to pay my respects as the jungle chorus continued to chirp around us.

World’s seas have hit hottest temperature on record for July, say scientists


Average sea surface temperature outside polar regions was highest on record for July, beating previous high in 2023




The world’s seas were hotter last month than in any July on record, scientists have said, as devastating heat struck western Europe.
Sea surface temperatures hit record highs for July on the Atlantic coast and western Mediterranean, the EU’s Copernicus climate change service found, with severe marine heatwaves roiling Europe’s seas. Globally, the average sea surface temperature outside the cold polar regions was the highest on record for the month, beating the previous July record set in 2023.








World’s oceans losing their greenness through global heating, study finds

Read more
Surface air temperatures around the world in July 2026 were marginally cooler than July 2024 – by just 0.01C – leading scientists to consider the two months as the joint-second warmest Julys on record.
Western Europe has experienced its hottest June-July period on record, data shows, with “exceptional” heat driving wildfires that devastated swathes of the Mediterranean.
The first two summer months of 2026 were 2.79C hotter than usual, the Copernicus said on Monday, beating the previous record set four years ago and reflecting the “exceptional persistence of heat” since the season began.
Central Europe is reeling from a heatwave in which national temperature records fell in a handful of countries including Austria and Slovakia. It is the latest in a scorching summer that has dried out vegetation and primed the continent to burn.
Samantha Burgess, a climate scientist at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, said this summer had been “a clear example” of climate breakdown intensifying extremes that reinforce each other.

“[As] persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over western Europe, the extreme temperatures also amplified widespread drought,” she said. “As soils dry out, they lose their ability to provide natural cooling, allowing heat to build more readily.”


Supercharged by fossil fuel pollution, a string of heatwaves have hit Europe since the end of spring, with particularly brutal heat at the end of June expected to have resulted in more than 10,000 deaths.
Copernicus said widespread dryness observed in May and June intensified last month, with exceptionally low rainfall and soil moisture in much of western Europe. Lake Mead plummets to historic low water level as Colorado River struggles


Levels at reservoir along Arizona-Nevada border dipped below previous record set in 2022, amid water crisis in west




Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, has plummeted to its lowest water level since it was filled some 90 years ago, the latest sign of a deepening water crisis in the American west.
Water levels at the reservoir, which straddles the Arizona-Nevada border outside Las Vegas, hit 1,040.4ft (317.1 meters) above sea level on Friday, according to federal data. That’s just below the record set on 28 July 2022, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation.

The reservoir is a critical storage system on Colorado River, a massive waterway that supplies roughly 40 million people across seven US states, tribal nations and Mexico, and irrigates millions of acres of farmland.







Water cuts loom as US unveils long-awaited response to Colorado River crisis

Read more
But the Colorado River basin is facing enormous pressure due to a combination of overuse, prolonged drought and extreme heat, and a lack of snowmelt to replenish the river. Lake Powell, the second major reservoir on the Colorado River, is also at historic low levels.
“It’s extremely significant and extremely concerning. You have three-quarters of the population of the Colorado River basin, some 30 million people, who are directly impacted by risks to Lake Mead,” said JB Hamby, the chair of the Colorado River board of California and a board member of the Imperial Irrigation District, the largest user of the river’s water. Hamby said it is vital for states that use Colorado River water to reduce water use.
Drought and dry conditions have stretched along the length of the Colorado and are particularly intense at its source in the Rocky Mountains.


View image in fullscreen
Water lines are visible on the rocky banks of Lake Powell on 1 August 2026 in Page, Arizona. Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
Melting snow provides important water for the river. This past winter, however, saw the worst snowpack on record for the Colorado River basin, adding more stress on farmers, industry, wildlife and hydropower producers, as well as the cities and towns that rely on the waterway.


Years of overuse combined with drought and rising temperatures have been depleting Lake Mead and Lake Powell, the country’s second-largest reservoir. Both are the lowest they have been in nearly seven decades.

The world’s most populous country needs state-generated demand to industrialise, decarbonise and avoid China’s overcapacity trap





India is attempting to do something the world has never seen before. So claimed Niti Aayog, the government of India’s policy thinktank, earlier this year. It said that no major economy has tried to expand GDP nearly eightfold within a generation while simultaneously redirecting its energy and industrial systems to reach net zero within two generations. Hence its detailed report’s claim that there is “no historical precedent”.
There is something to this. China industrialised at vast scale, but not on a sustainable net zero path. Korea, Japan and Europe became wealthy by industrialising before decarbonising. Today, rich nations have already satisfied the basic demands of their people and created the infrastructure and high per-capita energy use that India is still trying to build. The world’s most populous country has to do this while also reducing emissions.



The climate emergency is all too real for New Delhi. In April, on a single day, all of the planet’s top 50 hottest cities were in India. Yet the country still relies heavily on coal, especially at moments of peak power needs. This sets up a dangerous feedback loop: heat drives cooling demand; cooling demand drives coal-burning; coal‑burning drives temperatures higher. India is trying to change course. Non-fossil fuel sources now account for more than half of installed electricity capacity.
The report assumes India reaches $30tn GDP by 2047, with rising urbanisation, industrialisation and living standards. India’s net zero path will be judged politically by who bears the costs and who captures the gains. But the thinktank reasons that as India grows fast, so energy and infrastructure demand and investment rise too, and, voilà, India continues to grow fast. This may be a virtuous cycle. But left unexplained is what source of demand gets the process going and sustains it.
That requires a political economy of investment. It means explaining who spends first, who guarantees demand, how businesses are induced to keep building when existing factories are not fully used, and how private profitability is maintained when consumption’s share of national income falls.


India’s solar success partly answers these questions. In a 2025 paper, the political economist Mathias Larsen argues that India’s advances in sunlight-powered electricity came because the state created a market, used public sector financial firepower and protected domestic producers. That is not a story of private finance spontaneously allocating capital. It is a story of state-made demand.
But solar is one sector. A whole-economy transition may not work the same way. What happens when domestic demand can’t soak up the state-created capacity? While there are fears that people harvesting their food could put pressure on habitats, some ecologists suggest responsible foraging can boost conservation and biodiversity




Angus Morton crouches behind a cricket pavilion in a London park to snip stinging nettles from an unkempt patch of greenery.
“They’re so abundant and they’re so good,” says Morton, a regenerative gardener who pops out once a week to forage bits for dinner. “I use them in pesto, tea … I’ve even seen someone putting them in croquetas.”

Morton, who posts regularly about his foraging exploits online, is one of a growing number of people venturing into the wild in search of food. He says he shaves hundreds of pounds off his food bill each month, fermenting pine needles to carbonate drinks, picking ivy for soap and harvesting wild mushrooms for dinner.
But as reports of an early heatwave-ripened blackberry crop flood social media, he offers a warning.
“It’s important for this to thrive naturally,” he says, as he pours hot water over the leaves he gathered to make nettle tea. “As humans we should be working with it and not taking advantage of it. Only take what you need – about 10% of what’s there – so it has the chance to grow back. If you take more than you need, you’re going to ruin it.”
The increased popularity of foraging has prompted concern that pickers could put pressure on habitats and green spaces by over-harvesting fungi, flowers and fruit. Conservation groups advise foragers to take only small quantities, avoid rare species and leave enough for wildlife to consume.


View image in fullscreen
Forager Angus Morton making nettle tea. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian
Some have gone further by forbidding harvesting altogether. Last autumn, Surrey Wildlife Trust reminded visitors that mushroom picking was banned on its reserves to help protect fungi and the wildlife that depends on them. London Wildlife Trust also forbids picking at Walthamstow Wetlands, where wild plants, fruits and seeds provide food and habitat for birds and other animals.
But some foragers and ecologists argue that responsible gathering of wild food can help biodiversity by teaching people to recognise the nature around them – and give them a reason to protect it.
John Rensten, a foraging teacher and author of The Edible City: A Year of Wild Food, says foraging can be a biodiversity booster. “I believe in getting people to interact with landscape in order to want to protect it,” he says. “You feel connected towards it and you feel ownership of it and a desire to want to protect it and nurture it.”
Foraging teaches people about their environment, says Rensten, and this is the first step in battling biodiversity loss. He has seen as much delivering foraging courses. “The best comment we ever get from anybody is the guy who says, ‘I’ve been coming here 25 years and I’m never going to look at this place in the same way again.’

articles.jina_text:
Amid headlines about the UK’s drought, Europe’s wildfires and impossible global temperatures, it was 28C when I arrived in Slough last Monday. I was there to look around Slough Trading Estate, a place that might once have conjured up images of the TV comedy The Office, many of whose laughs came at the expense of this overgrown patch of suburbia, 20-odd miles west of London.
But these days, this area of town – an incongruous mixture of old-school businesses such as Mr Clutch and Angling Direct, and vast, metal-clad leviathans that look like something pulled from JG Ballard – has become a byword for the constant expansion of datacentres, those hulking symbols of the vast computing power that big tech now requires, not least because of the ever-more complex workings of artificial intelligence.



In many people’s minds, datacentres are also a byword for the two totemic issues of yet another searing summer: heat and water. Across the world, the huge amounts of electricity they demand, mostly generated using fossil fuels, indelibly connects them to the climate emergency. The constant machinations of their crammed-in servers require cooling processes that also use vast amounts of water. So it is that the 21st century’s dominant means of communication intensifies our era’s most terrifying threats.
The first building I loitered around was a datacentre owned by the California-based company Equinix. There were 100 or so cars in its “visitor” and “staff” spaces, no corporate branding to be seen – and, up close, the constant sound of a low industrial whirr. On the other side of the street, poetically enough, was a set of offices occupied by Thames Water, a few of whose employees were taking a break outside. I pointed across the road: did they know what the building contained?
“There’s loads of AI bits in there,” said a twentysomething woman called Louise. “I saw something about it on Instagram: all the water they use.” She rolled her eyes. “It’s ridiculous. Loads and loads of water because of all the AI.” On her phone, she found one of the posts she had seen. “Slough is quietly running Britain’s AI boom but there’s a problem,” it said. “When a heatwave hits, the machines get thirsty too. Cooling systems work overtime in hot weather, spiking demand for power and water.”
Someone suggested I make the five-minute journey to nearby Britwell, a housing estate built for bombed-out Londoners after the second world war. The first person I encountered was a mum from the area called Sheryl. “You notice the noise at night: like a whirring, buzzing sound,” she said. “And since we’ve had all these [new] ones up here, there seems to be more heat round here.”


Early research, including a recent preprint of a paper authored by researchers at Cambridge University earlier this year, does suggest that datacentres can have a “heat island” effect, pushing up temperatures in their immediate vicinity by an average of 2C, and as much as 9C. The huge fire was spotted in the early hours of the morning at the industrial estate in Dagenham (Picture: London Fire Brigade)



Firefighters continue to tackle a huge blaze at an east London waste site, with smoke visible for miles. 

The alarm was raised at about 3.26am today after the fire broke out at the site on Chequers Lane, Dagenham. 

Thick black smoke could be seen billowing into the air as flames engulfed the facility on the industrial estate near the A13. 

Local residents are urged to keep their windows and doors shut due to the smoke. 

Fifteen fire engines and around 100 firefighters are at the scene, London Fire Brigade said. 

They are using two turntable ladders, a hose laying unit and a high volume pump to try to access more water across the ground. 

Station Commander Graham Beers said: ‘This is a large incident that will see crews working hard through the morning to bring it under control. Residents in the nearby area should keep doors and windows closed where possible. The fire is producing a significant amount of smoke.’

The cause of the blaze is not known yet. No injuries have been reported. 

Crews and engines from Dagenham, Barking, East Ham and other surrounding fire stations were called to the blaze. 

The fire struck as London and large parts of the South are gripped by drought conditions, with a fifth heatwave of the season bringing more hot weather this week.

View image in fullscreen
