‘These are human fires, not wildfires’: Dunwich reflects on the devastation


As residents, nature wardens and experts consider the damage to the heathland and how to restore it, the climate crisis is foremost in their minds




A local community pulling together, emergency services saving homes and caravan parks from catastrophe, and farmers and nature reserve wardens working to rapidly create fire breaks to halt a marauding fireball 40 metres high – there was plenty to praise the week after a swathe of east Suffolk burned.
But local people were also in tears at the blackened, ruined state of more than 112 hectares (277 acres) of Dunwich Heath, mourning the devastation of a much-loved nature reserve alongside neighbouring Minsmere. The rare birds that inhabit the reserve have lost crucial habitat, while the rare invertebrate species there will have been “decimated”, according to the reserve staff.

The fire started on Wednesday 29 July; the cause is still unknown, but Suffolk Fire Service said the fire took hold at a “ferocious pace” owing to the hot weather, dry conditions and changing winds. More than 100 firefighters have attended the scene since then, and crews from 18 fire services were in attendance.


View image in fullscreen
A firefighter monitoring the situation near Dunwich Heath last week. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA
A week later, the above-ground fire has been subdued. The fire service has measured temperatures below ground exceeding 600C and surface temperatures of 60C. Hot winds and a lack of rain leave the dry, sandy region in a state of high alert for further outbreaks, with many evacuated residents advised not to return home. Locals and visitors have been kept away from an area of Dunwich Heath because the fire exposed unexploded ordnance from the second world war.


The impact on wildlife has been vicious. The reserve is home to some of the rarest bird species in the UK, including nightjars, nightingales and Dartford warblers. “The vegetation that is essential for supporting that birdlife, the structure of the gorse and the trees, all appears to have gone. So, in essence, the habitat they would rely on to nest, to feed, to shelter and to roost at night has gone, so they won’t have anywhere to return to,” said Adam Rowlands, the area manager for the RSPB.
As well as rare birds, the site is home to a wide range of rare invertebrates, including the narrow-mouthed whorl snail, antlions, and green tiger beetles.

Plastics contamination an ‘overlooked’ concern in food waste schemes, experts say


Researchers find microplastics can persist in compost, leaching into agricultural soils




Plastic contamination should be a central concern in efforts to deal with food waste, which campaigners call one of the most overlooked problems of the climate crisis, researchers have said.
This is despite the fact that, as the chef, author and activist Max La Manna puts it, food waste management is “one of the few climate problems where everyone wins”.

About one-third of all food produced worldwide is wasted each year, according to UN data. In the US, 40% of food waste goes to landfill, where it creates 30m metric tonnes of CO2 equivalent a year – more than Cuba’s total annual CO2 emissions in 2024, which amounted to 24.4m tonnes.
A new study, published in Nature Food, used life-cycle analysis modelling to compare the impacts – in terms of climate, nutrient pollution and plastic contamination – of different food-waste management scenarios.


The authors, based at the University of Vermont, compared the annual climate impacts of landfilled food waste with the climate impact of alternative recycling pathways and found that diverting food waste from landfill would reduce climate impacts by between 89% and 99%.
These non-landfill scenarios could also reduce nutrient pollution in water bodies – a process called eutrophication that occurs when excess nutrients result in algal blooms.
But the researchers also said that microplastics can persist in compost, which could lead to 20,000 tonnes contaminating US agricultural soils each year. To date, no study has looked at the “plastic pollution footprint” of different food-waste management strategies at national scale.
Kate Porterfield, the lead author, said the method was comparable to working out a “carbon footprint of a product or process”. Essentially, the researchers looked at the process of managing food waste and “tall[ied] up what the carbon emissions are across all of those life-cycle stages”, she said.
Porterfield said the large proportion of wasted food still in packaging “goes bad before it even reaches the consumer”. One approach to recycling food waste is using a mechanical “depacker”; the packaging then goes to landfill, while food waste goes to “beneficial reuse, like composting or anaerobic digestion”.

articles.jina_text:
The natural gas plant powering a sprawling Amazon data center project in Texas could become the largest climate polluter in the country, despite the company’s commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2040. 
As part of a planned data center campus in Pecos County, the tech giant is investing in an on-site natural gas power plant, the company has confirmed.
The plant is permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide per year, according to documents obtained by The New York Times and the climate research outlet Distilled. 





If the final plant matches those specifications, it would be the largest single source of climate pollution in the country, according to the Times, more than doubling the emissions from Alabama’s James H. Miller Jr. Power Plant, a coal facility which emits about 16 million tons of carbon dioxide annually. (Power plants don’t always emit the maximum they are allowed to, and the Amazon facility is still in early-stage construction.)
The company has emphasized that the power plant would not raise rates for Texas residents.

“Amazon believes in paying the full costs of powering our operations,” an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement to The Independent on Saturday. “Our new planned data center campus in Pecos County does just that: it’s powered by new on-site generation that won’t raise electricity costs for Texas families and designed to transition to grid-connected service as interconnection timelines allow.”
Amazon is “exploring opportunities for solar energy and battery storage on site,” according to the company. The Pecos project is expected to create “thousands of new jobs,” Amazon said.


The site is reportedly Amazon’s first major investment in off-grid power for a data center. 
This puts them in league with “hyperscalers” including Microsoft, Google and Meta, which have all invested in fossil fuel power sources this year as tech companies race to get enough data centers online to meet the ravenous demand for artificial intelligence. 
The data campus is the latest complication in Amazon’s highly touted climate commitments.
The company has long faced criticism for working with fossil fuel firms, and its emissions have largely continued to rise since it unveiled its climate commitment in 2019.

El Niño-generated storm waves crash onto seaside houses at Mondos Beach, California, on 12 January 2016. Photograph: Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty Images


‘Super El Niño’ could bring wet winter and flooding to western US, climate scientists warn


Weather system tied to warming sea surface expected to intensify in fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027




El Niño, a recurring climate phenomenon marked by above-average sea surface temperatures, when changes in wind patterns allow warmer water to spread across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, could spell a wet winter for portions of the western and south-eastern US, climate models show. Coastal areas may be at elevated risk of flooding, experts warn.
Climate scientists predict this year’s “super” El Niño, a label assigned when sea surface temperatures climb by at least 2C, will be the strongest of the century. The weather system is expected to intensify in the fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).








El Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of next year 

Read more
California has a 70%-100% chance of experiencing above-average rainfall along its coast, according to a model from the European center for medium-range forecasts.
“El Niño is never going to guarantee any particular outcome in any California winter,” Daniel Swain, the UCLA climate scientist, noted at a virtual El Niño town hall hosted by the California state senator Mike McGuire this week. But, he added, a weather event as strong as the one being currently predicted shifts the odds in favor of a wet winter: “That will likely affect and increase the likelihood of coastal flooding, particularly during strong storm events or during king tide events.”
California has been devastated by El Niños in the past.


A 1982-83 weather system destroyed 33 oceanfront homes and damaged 3,000 other residences, according to the California coastal commission. In a 1997-98 El Niño, California experienced massive flooding and 17 storm-related deaths. In more recent history, during the El Niño winter of 2015-16, state officials reported record coastal erosion on California beaches.
“With less beach in front of the coastline, the waves will have even greater impact on the shoreline with more likelihood of flooding and undercutting of cliffs,” said Mark Merrifield of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, at McGuire’s town hall.
El Niño is not expected to completely erase drought in the US south-west, where some reservoirs are at an all-time low. “It would have to be exceptionally wet,” Dr Joel Lisonbee, senior associate scientist at the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at the University of Colorado Boulder, told the Guardian in June

articles.jina_text:
Britain’s record-breaking summer of heatwaves and life-threatening extreme temperatures is only going to get worse each year unless we double down on efforts to tackle the climate crisis, experts have warned.
Back-to-back hot spells, which saw the mercury peak at 37.7C (99.9F) in June, have so far led to nearly 3,000 deaths, half of England and the whole of Wales are in drought and a failure to heed decades of warnings to build climate resilience into our supply chains has left the UK facing food shortages.
The news overseas is even more alarming, with unprecedented wildfires burning thousands of square kilometres of land around holiday resorts in Spain and France, claiming 16 lives, while record-low water levels threaten Europe’s industrial heartlands on the Rhine and exposing lost Nazi warships on the Danube.

People walk on a path between the sun-scorched grass, turned yellow-brown by a lack of rain, in London’s Greenwich Park (AFP/Getty)
And the picture is only set to intensify in the coming months as a record-breaking El Nino – a periodic warming of the Pacific Ocean – wreaks havoc with global weather systems, resulting in extreme rainfall in some parts of the world and devastating drought expected in others. 





Experts warn that recent temperatures are no anomaly, with worse to come unless we ramp up efforts to phase out fossil fuels and invest more heavily in renewable energy sources.

articles.title: Drought and scorching heatwaves threaten Europe’s vision of a nuclear-powered future
articles.raw_rss: Nuclear power offers Europe a reliable way of powering itself without laying waste to the planet. But hotter summers and a changing climate are interfering with how it works, writes James C. Reynolds
articles.raw_meta: Nuclear power offers Europe a reliable way of powering itself without laying waste to the planet. But hotter summers and a changing climate are interfering with how it works, writes James C. Reynolds
articles.jina_text:
It is an image that somehow captures the crisis of Europe’s present and future: a smouldering wildfire burning on grassland just two miles from a nuclear plant. 
More than 100 firefighters were called in to tackle the blaze sweeping through Dunwich Heath on the Suffolk coast at the end of July, which lies just north of the Sizewell B nuclear plant that powers up to 2.5 million British homes. The fire tore through the equivalent of 210 football pitches on the Suffolk coast before it was extinguished.
Across the continent, wildfires have been much more severe and widespread. Spain and France have seen tens of thousands of acres of land scorched over the last month, and nearly a quarter of a million people were forced from their homes. The Independent saw first-hand how communities have been torn apart as France recorded its hottest July on record.





It has left Europe in a bind. The continent urgently needs nuclear power to combat climate change; but extreme heat, drought and wildfires pose huge challenges for the transition.
As climate change brings hotter and more deadly summers, nuclear plants drawing water from drying rivers are struggling to keep their low-carbon nuclear fleets fully operational, resulting in outages and desperate moves to import electricity at a premium.

France had to close three reactors just last week after drought conditions cut flows in its rivers, while record-low waters levels on the Danube pushed Hungary to shut its sole nuclear plant, stretching power supply capacity to its limits.


Romania, meanwhile, blew up huge rocks and sank weighted barges in an effort to divert cooling water towards its nuclear plant on the Danube, after having to close one of two reactors last week. And Slovenia began reducing reactor output due to high temperatures and low flows on the Sava River. Serbia saw output at its largest hydropower plant fall to just 20 per cent of capacity, pressing the government to import electricity from abroad.
Experts say that while nuclear energy remains one of the most reliable and cost effective means of energy production, heat and drought linked to the climate crisis will create challenges for European nations to tackle in order to ensure a resilient grid ready for the future.

articles.jina_text:
The wreckage of a Nazi warship has become visible above the exceptionally low water line on the Danube near Prahovo in Serbia this week. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP
View image in fullscreen
The wreckage of a Nazi warship has become visible above the exceptionally low water line on the Danube near Prahovo in Serbia this week. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP


Nazi shipwrecks emerge from the depths as Europe’s Danube dries up


Unexploded ordnance and a military motorcycle also recovered following record heat and drought conditions




Record-low water levels in the Danube have exposed remnants of Europe’s Nazi past, with dozens of second world war ships emerging from the riverbed during an intense drought.
In the middle of the river on the Serbian and Romanian border, a broken-up hull was visible on a sandbank that is normally underwater. Other vessels were partly submerged, some still believed to be laden with weapons.



View image in fullscreen
The wreckage of a second world war German warship near Prahovo, Serbia on Tuesday. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP
The ships were part of Adolf Hitler’s Black Sea fleet that the German military deliberately sank towards the end of the war to slow down the Soviet advance. Historians say up to 200 German warships were scuttled in this way in September 1944. But Nazi Germany did not surrender until the following year in May 1945.





Sunken WWII era ships appear as Danube levels go down amid drought


The ships have been revealed during previous droughts only to disappear again as water levels rose along the second-longest river in Europe. The Serbian government has tried in the past to remove the wrecks, but most remain in place owing to the explosives they carried.


View image in fullscreen
The Serbian government has previously tried to remove wrecks such as the one pictured here near Prahovo. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP
Other second world war remnants have been found in other parts of the river, including a German military motorcycle in Budapest, Hungary.
In Slovakia, police recovered an unexploded British 1,543lb (700kg) bomb. Police said authorities loaded it on to a “specially modified firefighter vehicle with a sand bed, which ensured its safe transport” and took it to a 5-metre deep pit to detonate it.


View image in fullscreen
A second world war German military motorcycle is displayed at the defence ministry museum in Budapest, Hungary on Wednesday.  Photograph: Tamas Purger/EPA


In 1944, Britain’s Royal Air Force mined the river to disrupt enemy troops.
The Danube, which flows through 10 countries, has become increasingly difficult to navigate as low water levels create dangerous conditions. Prolonged droughts have left major European rivers at significantly lower water levels than is typical for the time of year, creating an energy crisis as many power plants rely on their natural water supply for cooling.

Scratch of the day: local football season postponed due to ‘rock hard’ pitches


Drought and record heat have forced the Norfolk and Suffolk league to move kick-off to the end of August as the ground is deemed too dangerous to play on




This summer’s record drought has forced a football league to delay the start of its season because “rock hard” pitches are a danger to its players.
The 2026/27 season in the Anglian Combination League of 85 amateur teams in Norfolk and Suffolk was due to start next weekend.

But on Friday after an urgent meeting, the league’s board announced it had unanimously decided to postpone the start of the season until the end of August, because most of the clubs’ pitches are dried out and too dangerous to play on.
It said a number of pre-season friendlies have had to be cancelled because of the drought and matches that have gone ahead have led to “many injuries”.
In a statement addressed to all leagues clubs, players and officials, it confirmed the start of the season will be delayed until 29 August.
“The rationale behind this decision is to protect the welfare of players, officials and all associated with the match day, in what has been the driest and hottest July since records began in 1836,” the league chair, Dale Brown, said in the statement. “Most of our league clubs pitches are grass and the ground conditions are extremely dry and pitches rock hard.”

Brown added: “This was a very difficult decision to reach and one that will not please all clubs.”
The league’s decision comes after a series of record-breaking heat waves and exceptionally low rainfall have left much of England and Wales visibly parched and the ground as hard as concrete.
Record temperatures were experienced in May and June, and July was the driest month since records began. A drought was declared in half of England last month with many water companies imposing hosepipe bans. Such a ban by Anglian Water which covers Norfolk and Suffolk, has been in force since 11 July.
Aerial images have shown dried out parks and sports fields devoid of any signs of green, with the exception of golf clubs, some sports clubs, and private schools who enjoy controversial exemptions from hosepipe bans.
The Met Office forecasts another heatwave next week, with temperatures set to reach 36C in parts of East Anglia and south-east England by next Thursday. There is no sign of much-needed rain, although humidity is expected to increase next week.

Report: Sadiq Khan calls on Andy Burnham to commit to climate action as pressure grows over North Sea oil 





Europe is burning. This summer, an unprecedented series of heatwaves has swept through the continent and across many parts of the globe. The consequences have been nothing short of catastrophic. In recent weeks deadly blazes have torn through France, Greece and Spain, killing firefighters, forcing people from their homes and robbing them of their livelihoods.
With Tuesday marking Britain’s 34th day of temperatures exceeding 30C (86F) this year, the UK has also found itself reckoning with ferocious heat. Wildfires have forced evacuations in Suffolk and the Cairngorms. In London – where parks have become burnt, brittle and brown – hundreds of grass fires have put our firefighters under pressure like never before. In July, the weather station at Kew Gardens recorded its first ever month without rain since it started operating in 1871. As rivers run dry and reservoirs run low, farmers are warning of food shortages amid the deepening drought. With thousands of deaths already estimated to be linked to the extreme heat we saw in May and June alone, it’s likely this figure will climb higher still.



The terrifying scenes we’ve seen so far this summer are the latest part of a pernicious long-term pattern. This is the third drought London has experienced in the past five years. Across the world, the past 11 years have been the 11 hottest ever recorded – and with a super strength El Niño forming in the Pacific which could pour yet more fuel on the fire, that trend is all but certain to continue. The climate emergency is here – and no one can say they didn’t see it coming.
When I was first elected mayor back in 2016, I warned that our rapidly warming world would be the defining challenge of our time. I was the first mayor of a global city to declare a climate emergency. Since then, a coalition of climate deniers and delayers has been relentless in condemning the green policies I’ve introduced. When I announced my intention to expand the Ulez – creating the largest clean air zone in the world – they unsuccessfully attempted to drag down the debate and whip up a crude culture war. On social media, people were blinded by a dark blizzard of disinformation designed to discredit climate action. Radicalised by what he’d seen online, one man even detonated a homemade bomb, destroying a Ulez camera in a shocking act of domestic terrorism.
Looking back now, it feels like the fierce fight over Ulez marked the beginning of something else: a new age of extreme climate scepticism. In the years since, the horrifying reality of the climate crisis has come into sharp relief – and yet somehow the clamouring voices of denial and delay have grown louder than ever. Writing in the Guardian, the mayor of London said that Andy Burnham’s administration must reaffirm its commitment to net zero and make clear it will continue to reduce the UK’s reliance on oil and gas “to get Britain back on track.”

There is growing concern among Labour MPs and climate experts that the new prime minister may support renewed drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea; since arriving in No 10, Burnham has remained largely tight-lipped on climate and environmental concerns despite speaking out about them during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester.

Khan writes that, faced with the realities of a rapidly worsening climate crisis, which has amplified heatwaves and droughts sweeping across the UK and Europe, governments must redouble their efforts.
“National governments across the globe must step up and meet the gravity of this moment with renewed focus, funding, and resolve,” said Khan.
A decision on whether to approve more drilling in the North Sea is expected in the coming weeks. The Labour manifesto committed the party to halting any new licences. Two projects – the Jackdaw gasfield and the Rosebank oilfield – were granted permission under the Conservatives, but operations were paused after a court challenge by environmental groups.
The new energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is expected to make decisions on Jackdaw and Rosebank after consultations regarding their emissions conclude in the coming weeks.

“Things are more unsettled already, back to more like normal summer weather, and there will be some rain around next week.”  
That will be mainly in northern Britain, however. In the south, “almost entirely dry conditions” are expected to continue for weeks and there could be more extreme heat this month.  
It means some places could be in drought for several more weeks at least. 
The UK had an unprecedented heatwave in May, before the hottest June day on record with a peak of 36.1°C. That was followed by the sunniest and driest July ever known in England and Wales, with just 10 per cent of the average rainfall throughout the month. 



 
The UK’s rainfall since the start of June is just 51 per cent of what we would expect across an average summer, albeit with a few weeks of the season still to come.  
“It is definitely going to be right up there as one of the most remarkable summers,” says Lang. But what could the impacts be? 

Water levels are low at Lockwood Reservoir near Walthamstow in north London (Photo: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty) 
How this compares to 1976’s scorching summer  
Some people have drawn comparisons with the infamous summer of 1976 when people had to queue for water from communal standpipes.  
This summer is nowhere near the country’s driest, however, and the UK is unlikely to face the challenges of 50 years ago for several important reasons.  
Because of a wet start to June, the UK has had a national average of 130.2mm of rain so far this summer, which is already well above the 107.3mm of 1976 – and the record low of 105.9mm in 1995.  
It’s often forgotten that the scorching summer of 1976 was the climax of a far longer drought. The dry period began in May the previous year. The following 16 months were the driest period of such a length for over 200 years.  
In contrast, 2026 began with one of the wettest winters on record and warnings of flood risks. Plus, we’re better able to manage supplies these days. 



 
“Investments in upgraded network infrastructure enable companies to move water more effectively between regions compared to the isolated systems of 50 years ago,” says Rob Wilby, professor of hydroclimatic modelling at Loughborough University. He adds that leakage has fallen by 43 per cent since privatisation in 1989, according to Ofwat.

Andy Burnham is said to be preparing to ease several of Labour's Net Zero commitments in response to the cost of living crisis.
Rules around electric car sales could be significantly weakened, potentially allowing half of all new vehicles sold by 2030 to still have petrol engines.


Right now, only 20 per cent of new cars sold that year will be allowed to run on fossil fuels.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has indicated she will not stick to her predecessor Ed Miliband's target of nearly eliminating fossil fuels from Britain's power supply by 2030 if doing so would push up household bills.

Ms Fahnbulleh warned The Times of an "affordability challenge" facing hard-working Britons which ministers will have to address.
She indicated the clean power target, commonly panned as 'Net Stupid Zero lunacy' by Reform UK's Richard Tice, could be let slip by a year or two if that meant lower costs for consumers.
"We need to keep momentum [towards clean power]," she said. "But we've also got to do it in a way that works for people. And that is about affordability."

articles.raw_meta: This year’s El Niño weather pattern is to blame, according to scientists
articles.jina_text:
The remaining months of the Atlantic hurricane season could be relatively quiet, a new federal prediction shows - but not everywhere is as lucky. 
There are between 2 and 6 hurricanes, 0 and 2 major hurricanes, and 7 to 13 named storms expected in the Atlantic for the rest of the year, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said on Thursday.
That’s a slight reduction from an initial forecast issued in May and lower than the average season, though it only takes one major storm to threaten lives.





Precipitation below average along the eastern and southern shores is tied to an El Niño Climate pattern, NOAA said.
This pattern is also what’s responsible for an above-average hurricane year in the Pacific season, which sees storms hit Hawaii and along the West Coast.






open image in gallery
This image of Tropical Storm Bertha moving along the Gulf Coast was captured by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s GOES East satellite last month. NOAA just issued an updated outlook for the Atlantic season showing more below-normal activity in the basin - but a different story elsewhere (NOAA Satellites)





open image in gallery
Kids play in the floodwaters from Tropical Storm Bertha in New Orleans, Louisiana, last month. The storm was one of two named storms in the Atlantic this year (AP)





open image in gallery
Children play near breaking waves from Tropical Storm Bertha in New Orleans, Louisiana, last month. There have been no hurricanes in the Atlantic yet (AP)
Plus, this year’s El Niño is particularly strong - it’s being called a “super” or “Godzilla” El Niño, boosted by excess heat stored in Earth’s oceans.


Hurricanes need warm ocean temperatures to form, and record temperatures in the Atlantic have supercharged some of the biggest hurricanes in recent years.
“When El Niño emerges, it usually becomes the dominant factor in total hurricane season activity, and this El Niño continues to get stronger every month,” Matt Rosencrans, lead hurricane season forecaster with NOAA’s National Weather Service, explained in a statement.





open image in gallery
Brad Reinhart, Senior Hurricane Specialist, works on tracking Tropical Storm Arthur at the National Hurricane Center in June in Miami, Florida. NOAA says El Nino has been behind below-normal Atlantic hurricane activity (Getty Images)
Other mechanisms that determine the number and intensity of tropical storms in the Atlantic play a smaller role, he noted.



That’s why the outlook for the Eastern Pacific hurricane season is unchanged, with 15-22 named storms and the Central Pacific basin could see between 5-13 named storms.





So far, there have been seven named storms in the Eastern Pacific, including two that became hurricanes named Fausto and Genevieve.

articles.jina_text:
Two councillors have come under fire in west London after being accused of climate change denial amid a drought in London.




In a Facebook comment, Councillor Darshan Nagi, the Conservative councillor for Hounslow East, described climate change as a “natural process.” He added: “It started from ice age and haz been happening since upto now and it will carry on NOTHING WILL STOP IT.”








“ALL THESE ORGANISATIONS WHO ARE HYPING UP CLIMATE CHANGE AND TAKING MONEY IN DIFFERENT TAXES AND [CHARGES] AND PAYING THEMSELVES HIGH WAGEZ AND GIVING FUNDING TO MULTINATIONAL COMPANIES TO PREVENT [CLIMATE] CHANGE. I WOULD CALM THEM………….”




Cllr Nagi’s comment was made below a post on Brentford Today reporting on the Leader of Hounslow Reform, Cllr Tony Brown, reposting tweets which say “climate emergency is a big hoax.”




Cllr Jack Emsley, Leader of the Hounslow Conservative Group, told the Local Democracy Reporting Service [LDRS] that this is not the view of the wider group, nor was it policy. 


Councillor Tony Brown, Hounslow Reform Leader
Hounslow Council




In a written statement, Cllr Nagi said that his comment was clumsy, and rejects the assertion that he said climate change is not real.













He said: “The comment on Facebook doesn’t represent the view of the party or the Conservative Group. I was trying to convey that climate change is a big process that won’t be stopped by one country alone pursuing net zero.




“I appreciate my comment was quite clumsy, but at no point have I said climate change isn’t real – rather, the current policies that the government claims are supposed to tackle climate change are in fact about raising revenue as opposed to mitigating the impact of our changing climate.”









When approached by the LDRS about his reposts on X which claim that climate change is a hoax and implied scientists are “hiding something from you”, Cllr Brown said his view on the matter is “quite nuanced.” He added: “The fact that I have liked a tweet does NOT make it my definitive position on the subject.




“What I do believe is that prosperity through growth makes any society much more effective in being able to mitigate climate change. And it is in that context that net zero measures having given us the highest industrial electricity prices in the world is doubly unfortunate.

“Declarations of climate emergency are more performative than substantial and risk wasting hard-pressed taxpayer’s money. The future with AI is looking very energy intensive. A controversial “bottle tax” is putting thousands of jobs, and even British beer itself, at risk, Andy Burnham was warned.
Brewer, unions and glass manufacturers presented cases of ‘Burnham’s Brew’, a specially created IPA, to Number 10 Downing Street and also to the Prime Minister’s Number 10 North, in Manchester.


They say that the Extended Producer Responsibilty (EPR), or ‘bottle tax’, which was introduced as a Net Zero initiative, is a threat to the glass sector and brewing industry.
The EPR puts the financial onus on dealing with waste on the businesses behind the packaging, rather than councils. But it is charged by weight, and because glass is heavy it can attract a higher cost.

The GMB union has warned unless the fees – the highest rates in Europe – are reduced, factories could close.
EPR cost brewers £124m last year. Brewers and glass manufacturers believe the tax will also impact investment in the UK.


‘Burnham’s Brew’ is intended to highlight the 4,750 jobs that British Glass, the British Beer and Pub Association and the GMB say are at risk because of EPR.

A petition was also handed into Downing Street by workers concerned about their jobs.

View image in fullscreen
Solar panels arranged on the rooftop of an industrial park in Jimo, Qingdao, in eastern China's Shandong province. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images


Trump orders new 15% tariff on key material for solar panels and microchips


Move to raise levy on goods made with polysilicon aims to protect domestic US supply chains from China, the major producer




Donald Trump has ordered a new 15% tariff on imported products made of polysilicon, an important ingredient in microchip manufacturing that is primarily produced by China.
The new tariff, which will take effect on 4 December, is aimed at supporting US chip and solar panel supply chains to compete with Beijing on artificial intelligence and energy.

The executive order signed by the president on Thursday evening said: “The plan of action in ⁠this proclamation will, among other things, help ensure the commercial viability of United States production of polysilicon and its derivatives that is necessary to meet United States economic and national security requirements.”
Polysilicon, an ultra-pure form of silicon, is an important ingredient in making the semiconductors vital for AI processing power, datacentres and solar power generation.
US solar factories have long accused Chinese ‌rivals of dumping cheaper panels on the ‌market, which they say have been enabled by excessive government subsidies and by moving manufacturing to other countries to dodge US tariffs.
China’s foreign affairs ministry hit back at the latest measures, accusing the US of “overstretching the concept of national security, and abusing state power to go after Chinese businesses”.


View image in fullscreen
Solar panels advance toward final testing at a First Solar manufacturing facility in Perrysburg, Ohio, US. Photograph: Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images
“Protectionism will not make the US more competitive,” the spokesperson Lin Jian said, arguing that the move “seriously disrupts normal trade and economic exchanges between Chinese and US businesses, and is not in the interest of US businesses and consumers or anyone else for that matter”.


“China will continue firmly protecting our businesses’ legitimate and lawful rights and interests,” Lin added.
The US has two main polysilicon factories, including Hemlock Semiconductor, which operates ‌a plant in Michigan and is a joint venture between the US tech company Corning and Japan’s Shin-Etsu Handotai. The Munich-based Wacker Chemie runs a factory in Tennessee.
A spokesperson for Corning said the new tariff encouraged “continued investment in US capacity and supports long-term US competitiveness”, while Wacker said it appreciated the administration’s engagement “given the ramifications for semiconductor supply chain resilience, advanced computing infrastructure, and broader US defence and security interests”.

articles.jina_text:
Temperature records have been broken in several countries across central and eastern Europe as the extreme weather that has caused wildfires and droughts across the continent continues.
Countries including Slovakia, Austria and Hungary registered record temperatures. On Thursday, the Slovakian hydrometeorological agency said a new high of 42C (108F) had been reached in Dolné Plachtince.

Authorities in Poland were forced to shut down the Kozienice and Połaniec coal-fired power plants after critically low water levels in the Vistula River limited cooling water supplies. The disruption removed about 1.3GW of capacity from Poland’s power system.
On Wednesday, the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, had urged employers to look after their staff and provide air conditioning and cold water.


View image in fullscreen
Low water levels in Poland’s Vistula River on Thursday. Photograph: Wojtek Jargiło/EPA
In Germany, climate activists demanding an end to the use of fossil fuels demonstrated outside the chancellery against the lack of government action to keep people safe from extreme heat. An estimated 11,900 people across the country have died from heat this summer, according to new estimates from the Robert Koch Institute.


“This extreme heat and its consequences are the result of a fossil fuel policy that is completely irresponsible and extremely dangerous,” said Annkatrin Schwirten, from Fridays for Future Berlin. “We must not become accustomed to thousands of heat-related deaths every summer.”
The Hungarian prime minister, Péter Magyar, wrote on X on Thursday that the nuclear power station which had been temporarily powered down would be going back online.
“Good news: we are already nine centimeters above the Danube’s Sunday low point, and rain is expected in the Austrian catchment areas,” he wrote. “One of the turbines at the Paks nuclear power plant is operating. Regardless of this, on today’s hot day there will still be a strong need for voluntary reductions in electricity consumption.”
The brutal heat and continuing drought conditions are being supercharged by the escalating climate crisis, and experts warn these are putting huge pressure on local populations, critical infrastructure and wildlife across the region.
Paweł Pomian, from EKO-UNIA, a Polish environmental organisation, said “power plants driving climate change were increasingly becoming its victims”, adding that the impact of this summer’s extreme conditions, fuelled by the burning of fossil fuels, should be a “wake-up call not only for Poland, but for the whole of Europe”.


“The faster we develop wind and solar power – technologies that require the least water to generate electricity – the better we can protect both energy security and our rivers,” he said.

articles.jina_text:
Firefighters battle smoke and flames as a wildfire sweeps through West Attica in Greece. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Firefighters battle smoke and flames as a wildfire sweeps through West Attica in Greece. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images


Why Britain is breathing the world’s wildfire smoke


Scientists say global blazes account for 10% of UK’s particle pollution – and climate crisis could make the problem worse




Smoke rising above wildlife habitats, thousands of people evacuated and homes and livelihoods reduced to ashes – this is fast becoming the defining image of Britain and European summers.
Dr Mark Parrington, a senior scientist at the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, said: “Recent wildfires in south-western Europe produced large quantities of smoke, which caused significant degradation air quality across southern France and central regions of Spain.

“This was particularly notable in the cities of Bordeaux and Madrid, which were immediately downwind of the largest wildfires, in Gironde and Ávila respectively, with local measurements of PM2.5 indicating concentrations well above the air quality guidelines.”
Researchers at the University of Edinburgh and UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology have been tracking wildfire smoke reaching Britain. They found that wildfires – including some thousands of miles away – account for about 10% of the UK’s particle pollution.









0:59

Firefighters in Spain and France battle raging wildfires – video
Damaris Tan, at the University of Edinburgh, created a computer simulation of global wildfires and agricultural burning. She said: “While wildfires may not impact air pollution in the UK as acutely as other countries, wildfires globally add to the UK population’s long-term health burden. The relative importance of this is likely to increase in the future.”


The study found that large fires anywhere in the northern hemisphere could increase UK air pollution. “Time lags on the scale of months are possible,” Tan said. “It depends on the location of the wildfires relative to the UK and the meteorology, but it took over three months for the effects of 2018 wildfires to become negligible to 2019 concentrations in the UK.”
Prof Mathew Heal, at the University of Edinburgh and part of the study team, said: “To meet legal targets for particle pollution, the UK may need to over-deliver on the emission reductions to allow for the potential of increased wildfires in the future.”
In 2019, almost half of the wildfire pollution in the UK originated from fires in Russia. Tan said: “The UK got significant contributions from both directions, on winds from the east and also from the west via circulation around the globe.”
In the northern hemisphere, Canadian fires dominated in 2023 and continued to have a significant impact over the following two years. Tan said: “The Canadian contribution to the UK in 2024 and 2025 was likely more than double that of most years prior to 2023.”

While corporate Britain was hiring armies of sustainability consultants to write glossy reports, Mark Sait was quietly getting on with the job and knocking millions of pounds off the energy bills of the nation's hotels, hospitals and schools.
The founder of SaveMoneyCutCarbon is refreshingly honest about his motivations. Ask him if he has always been an environmentalist and the answer is a flat "no".


What drives him and his multi-million-pound business is a simple proposition: help other people save money. 
Speaking exclusively to GB News, he shared: "If you walk into a business and ask: 'Do you want to cut carbon?' There'd be a very small proportion of people who knew what you were talking about. 

Speaking exclusively to GB News, Mr Strait shared how his business has helped other companies save money and cut carbon  | 
GETTY / SAVE MONEY CUT CARBON 


"But if you ask: 'Do you want to knock 25 per cent off your energy bill?' Everyone understands that."
He puts the same challenge to people today. Everyone knows what £1,000 off a household energy bill looks like, or £100,000 off a commercial one. 
However, he noted that: "If I say to someone: 'What does a ton of carbon look like?' Most people will reply that they do not know".

Through his consultancy firm, Mr Sait provides other firms with guidance on how they can both cut costs and save the environment by introducing Net Zero-friendly technologies to their operations.
The story begins in a Los Angeles bar. Some 15 years ago, Mr Sait was running a business spun out of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, working alongside "incredibly intelligent people that put men on the moon and built satellites." 
Over a beer one evening, one of them predicted the world would soon be gripped by rows over carbon emissions and that conflict over water shortages would follow.

articles.title: The 132 worst rivers in England for pollution – and the four that are clean
articles.raw_rss: Precious chalk streams among the most polluted of the country's waterways
articles.raw_content:
Precious chalk streams and rivers polluted by mining are among the water bodies that have been branded the worst in England following six years of extensive research by the Environment Agency (EA).



On Thursday the EA published its latest classifications for England’s 4,658 surface water bodies, which includes rivers, lakes, estuaries and groundwater. 



These water bodies are split into five categories: high, good, moderate, poor or bad. 



Just 14.3 per cent were found to be at least good ecological health, while none were found to be in good chemical health. 



These classifications are published every six years and are based on a range of factors, including fish and invertebrate populations, as well as nutrient and chemical pollution. 



Rivers are broken down into individual sections based on physical factors, for example when they are joined by a large tributary. 



Of the 3,772 river sections classified by the EA, 132 (three per cent) were found to be in the worst possible condition, meaning its ecosystems are severely damaged and fail to support biodiversity.









A number of chalk streams are on the list, including the Gypsey Race in Yorkshire, Chalk Beck in Cumbria and Devils Brook in Dorset.



Chalk streams are a rare type of river that rise from underground springs in landscapes with chalk bedrock. There are only 210 chalk streams globally and 85 per cent of them are in England.

articles.jina_text:
On Thursday the EA published its latest classifications for England’s 4,658 surface water bodies, which includes rivers, lakes, estuaries and groundwater.  
These water bodies are split into five categories: high, good, moderate, poor or bad. 

 
Just 14.3 per cent were found to be at least good ecological health, while none were found to be in good chemical health.  
These classifications are published every six years and are based on a range of factors, including fish and invertebrate populations, as well as nutrient and chemical pollution.  
Rivers are broken down into individual sections based on physical factors, for example when they are joined by a large tributary.  
Of the 3,772 river sections classified by the EA, 132 (three per cent) were found to be in the worst possible condition, meaning its ecosystems are severely damaged and fail to support biodiversity.



 

 
  
A number of chalk streams are on the list, including the Gypsey Race in Yorkshire, Chalk Beck in Cumbria and Devils Brook in Dorset. 
Chalk streams are a rare type of river that rise from underground springs in landscapes with chalk bedrock. There are only 210 chalk streams globally and 85 per cent of them are in England.  
Chalk acts as a purifier meaning the water should be exceptionally clean, but many have become badly polluted.  
Feargal Sharkey, the former Undertones front man who is a passionate defender of chalk steams, told The i Paper “you can see the degradation” in England’s rare rivers.  
“When it comes to our chalk streams some of these that are not meeting the good ecological status are now nothing more than grassy ditches running through the open countryside,” he said. 

A stretch of the River Tees at its source in the North Pennines is one of just four stretches of water classified as high for good ecological health (Photo: Getty) 
Many of the rivers classified as bad will be suffering due to sewage pollution, such as the River Wandle, a tributary of the Thames in south London. 
However, others are failing due to other reasons such as the Ashfoldshide Beck in North Yorkshire, which is badly polluted with heavy metals due to historic lead mining. 



 
The East and West Fen Drains in Lincolnshire are also on the list, artificial waterways that are heavily polluted due to agriculture.  
Just four sections of river achieved the highest possible ecological standard, including Barrow Burn and Ridless Burn, two streams within Northumberland National Park. 
A stretch of the River Tees at its source in the North Pennines was also classified as high, as well as a stretch of the River Till from its source in Northumberland.

Of 3,772 river sections assessed, 132 (3%) were rated in the worst possible 'bad' condition, including several rare chalk streams such as the Gypsey Race in Yorkshire and Devils Brook in Dorset. Only four river stretches received the highest 'high' ecological rating, with sewage pollution identified as a key driver of poor water quality.

Trump administration to pay German firm $1.22bn to cut offshore wind leases


Agreement with RWE is fifth deal Trump team has made with energy companies, offering payouts to give up projects




The German energy company RWE has reached a $1.22bn deal with the US government to relinquish its offshore wind leases and instead redirect funds towards fossil fuel investments.
The agreement marks the fifth deal the Donald Trump administration has struck with energy companies, offering payouts in exchange for abandoning renewable energy projects and redirecting investment towards fossil fuels.

This latest deal takes it to almost $4bn of taxpayer money spent on killing offshore wind projects.
Announcing the deal with the US interior department on Thursday, RWE said it had agreed to give up its offshore wind leases off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana.


“After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the US for the foreseeable future,” the company said, referring to the leases it initially secured with a “long-term commitment to develop offshore wind capacity”.
RWE paid $1.1bn for its New York lease in a 2022 auction held by the Joe Biden administration, while its leases in Louisiana and California cost a combined $163m, Reuters reports.
“The settlement resolves RWE US Offshore’s legal claims and provides $1.22 billion in settlement funds,” RWE continued, adding that the deal would allow it to “direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”
As part of the agreement, RWE will spend $900m to acquire a 16% stake in an unnamed Louisiana liquified natural gas (LNG) project. The company said the settlement proceeds would be used to fund construction of the terminal.
RWE has also signed a $300m turbine reservation agreement under which it will develop a pipeline of 15 natural gas peaker plants across the country.
The interior secretary, Doug Burgum, hailed the deal, saying on Thursday: “We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power, and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country’s long-term energy future.”


The RWE agreement appears to be the largest deal the Trump administration has struck with an energy company to kill clean energy projects. Earlier agreements with other companies, including TotalEnergies and Duke Energy, amounted to $2.7bn in taxpayer money.

Human-driven climate crisis fuels Canada’s deadly wildfires, study finds


Current blazes roaring across country more than twice as likely to occur because of fossil fuel-driven global heating




The human-driven climate crisis made the conditions that led to blazes roaring across Canada, which have caused toxic smoke to spew throughout the country and into the US, twice as likely to occur, a new analysis has found.
Heightened global temperatures, caused by the burning of fossil fuels, amplified the risk of fire-prone weather in Ontario and the Northwest Territories, scientists found. These provinces have been racked by fires this summer, causing towns to be evacuated and unhealthy smoke to unfurl across multiple cities in North America.

There are currently nearly 700 fires ablaze across Canada, with a huge 3.8m hectares of the country, mainly in its sprawling boreal forests. But the study by World Weather Attribution, a consortium of scientists that analyses climate change’s influence upon extreme events, found that fire weather seen in Canada this year is no longer a rare event.



The climate-influenced conditions that dry out vegetation and soils, making them more prone to combustion, are now expected every two to six years in the Northwest Territories and every six to 15 years in Ontario. If humanity hadn’t overheated the planet by burning coal, oil and gas, the scientists determined, such extreme fire conditions would occur less than once every 40 years.
Canada, which has a quarter of the world’s boreal forests, has always experienced fire. But the climate crisis has made fire conditions more extreme and since 2023, when huge fires also spread across Canada, the country has suffered a “fundamentally different” scale and intensity of blazes, according to Theodore Keeping, an expert in extreme weather at Imperial College London and part of the WWA research team.


View image in fullscreen
The Brunswick Creek wildfire from Boston Bar, British Columbia, Canada, on 7 July 2026. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images


“The geographic spread of these fires is scary and shows that despite preparedness from wildfire governance, adaptation alone is not enough,” Keeping said. “We need to rapidly move away from fossil fuels to avoid events like this becoming even more of a reality.”
The WWA group finalized the study of Canada’s fire conditions shortly after unveiling findings showing the climate crisis had an even larger role in record fires raging in Spain and France, which has staged its largest ever peacetime evacuation due to the flames.

NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper


Health secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demand 
 
 
Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather? 




The NHS has been warned to prepare for potential annual summer crises caused by extreme heat with the same pressures as winter, as heatwaves caused by the climate crisis become routine in the UK.
The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said NHS staff were feeling A&E pressures that would normally be expected only during flu season – and said the government would use major investment in NHS infrastructure to tackle the health service’s resilience to high summer temperatures.

Doctors and other medical professionals have warned of the impact that repeated heatwaves are having on the NHS in England, including advice from the Royal College of GPs to cancel surgeries in extreme weather. Radiotherapy machines and MRI scanners have failed in hot weather, wards have overheated and cooling units serving hospitals have broken down.
England is on track to record its highest number of heat-related deaths this summer, with an estimated 2,877 people dying in the May and June heatwaves.
Summers are likely to become increasingly hot in the future, with temperatures topping 40C likely to become more frequent instead of being outliers as the climate crisis takes further hold.

Cooper told the Guardian that rising global temperatures were causing challenges for the NHS that it had not encountered before. “This is a new thing for the NHS to have to deal with. There is a remarkable determination of the NHS to respond, but we need much greater resilience.”


She said that in her new role as health secretary she had visited her local A&E in Yorkshire where staff described the overcrowding caused by heatwaves. “It would be normal during the winter weeks and months, but not in the summer, to have the very high attendances that they have had,” she said.
She said she had discussed a public health awareness campaign with the chief medical officer, Sir Chris Whitty, warning people to look out for elderly relatives and those with young babies to ensure they were coping in the heat.
Climate change meant “some immediate acute responses”, Cooper said, adding: “I’ve been clear we now need to prepare for summer pressures in the way that the NHS for a long time has prepared for winter pressures.
“We need a much clearer assessment now of what that means, what the pressures are going to be, what management needs to be in place to cope.”

London bus drivers plan to go on strike later this month over their working conditions, as many have been experienced cab temperatures reaching close to 40C in the recent heat. Most London buses are fitted with air-flow cooling systems rather than air conditioning. Sadiq Khan, the mayor, has said drivers should not be working in unsafe hot conditions, but Arriva, the private operator, has said it will take time to update its fleet.
Rail services have also been disrupted as the shrinkage of soil due to the dry weather has made embankments unsafe in the south of England because sleepers, part of the tracks, can move or drop out of position. Heat can also warp rails, leading operators to impose lower speed limits for safety.
On the roads, the RAC has reported that breakdowns have soared by a fifth, often owing to engines overheating, or tyre blowouts on overheated road surfaces.


View image in fullscreen
A London bus driver takes a break in the shade on a day the weather exceeded 30C. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
Farming and food
This year’s harvest could be the worst on record, analysis published on Wednesday found, as the third year running of drought in England left farmers with dry soil and damaged crops. Cereals and oilseed yields could be down as much as 2.5m tonnes across the UK, worth £390m in lost revenue for arable farmers, according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank. Livestock farmers are also under pressure: grass growth has halved, forcing some to use feed they had hoped to save for winter.


This followed an unusually wet start to the year but most farms are not in a position to store water adequately on their farms. The Country Land and Business Association (CLA), representing landowners, is calling for planning reforms to make small reservoirs on farms easier, while some regenerative farming practices can also help to store more water on land.

“For far too long, Radical Climate Activists attempted to hold our Great Country hostage by drastically and unreasonably expanding the intended scope of the Endangered Species Act,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Tuesday. 
“This was complete and total regulatory overreach by unelected bureaucrats! They treated Americans very unfairly by stifling the production of important resources like Oil, Natural Gas, and Timber, and blocking the construction of family homes and critical Infrastructure.”





“Even our Military couldn’t train on land that was deemed ‘off limits’ to protect a little rodent!“ he complained.
“Now my Administration has returned the Endangered Species Act to how it was intended to be, just as the Great Justice Antonin Scalia has explained in previous cases.

The U.S. Supreme Court upheld the Endangered Species Act’s definition of ‘harm’ in a 1995 ruling to protect spotted owls but the Trump administration has now moved to revise the rules (Alan Dyck/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the approach to the law had “turned routine activity into a regulatory trap, drove up costs that impacted people’s lives, and expanded federal authority beyond what Congress intended.
“For years, federal agencies abused the ESA to obstruct lawful land use and burden American families and businesses.”

articles.title: Prioritise new jobs over green targets to win public contracts, firms told
articles.raw_rss: The changes are part of government efforts to tackle the youth unemployment crisis.
articles.raw_meta: The changes are part of government efforts to tackle the youth unemployment crisis.
articles.jina_text:
Andy Burnham will tell firms bidding for public contracts to prove they are creating jobs rather than meeting green and social targets in a bid to get more people into work.
The prime minister will overhaul the £90bn public procurement system so bidders have to show they are supporting young people into work and addressing local skills shortages.
It comes as the government seeks to tackle the youth unemployment crisis, with Burnham saying he wants to create "growth in every postcode".
But green groups criticised the plans, arguing supporting young people into work should not come at the expense of the environment.
Companies bidding for government contracts are judged on a range of measures, including value for money and the extent to which they bring benefits to the local community. 
Under the changes, the weighting given to the benefits brought by companies will be doubled, from 10% to 20% for contracts worth £5m or more, the Cabinet Office said. 
Previously, this accounted for how companies created social value through measures such as equality and diversity, net zero and the post-Covid recovery. 
The new 20% measure will instead be based on job creation. Bidders will be given extra credit for creating local jobs paying above the minimum wage, plugging local skills gaps by offering training and particularly by offering 45-day work experience placements for young people. 
Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show more than a million people aged 16 to 24 are currently not in education, employment or training (Neet).
Burnham used a similar initiative to oversee a rise in the latter during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester. 
First Secretary of State Louise Haigh — who is effectively Burnham's deputy prime minister — said the procurement process in its current form was a "tick-box exercise".
"Every pound of taxpayer money should be spent in a way that benefits local communities — creating good jobs and giving young people the skills they need for the future," she said.
The new model will apply to both British and international firms bidding for public contracts.
Haigh said: "These new rules will ensure the £90 billion that is spent each year through government contracts supports British jobs, skills and people in every postcode."
Cabinet Office Minister Mark Ferguson said that businesses who secure government contracts "have a responsibility to give back".
"Businesses that benefit from the billions of taxpayer pounds spent by government, will have to create more local jobs and opportunities for young people in their area," he said.
But Greenpeace UK's head of politics Ami McCarthy said protecting the environment and helping young people into work are "mutually beneficial and one shouldn't come at a cost to the other".
"Companies should be held to account with environmental targets to help achieve a better future without leaving young workers behind," they added.

articles.title: UN warns monster El Niño could push 49 million more people into hunger
articles.raw_rss: Global acute food insecurity projected to rise to 274 million people across 45 countries, WFP says
articles.raw_meta: Global acute food insecurity projected to rise to 274 million people across 45 countries, WFP says
articles.jina_text:
A powerful El Niño weather pattern could push nearly 49 million more people into acute hunger by the end of next year, the U.N. World Food Programme warned Wednesday, raising fears of worsening food shortages across some of the world's most vulnerable regions.
The agency said there is an 81% chance of a very strong El Niño developing, with Pacific Ocean temperatures on track to reach their highest levels since at least 1982. If forecasts hold, it could become the strongest El Niño since 1950, triggering widespread droughts, floods and erratic rainfall that threaten food production.
Based on an assessment of 45 countries most vulnerable to El Niño, the WFP estimates the number of people facing acute food insecurity could climb by almost 49 million, bringing the total to about 274 million. Central America and Southern Africa are expected to be among the hardest-hit regions, with food insecurity projected to increase by 83% and nearly 75%, respectively. Southern Africa, South America and the Caribbean could each see more than 12 million additional people fall into acute hunger.





open image in gallery
Tourists cool off at a public water fountain in Paris, June 26 (Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.)
"These are events that in the past have triggered large-scale hunger," Jean-Martin Bauer, director of the WFP's Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Service, told reporters.





Bauer said global food supplies are entering the El Niño period in relatively good shape after strong harvests in recent years, but warned that conflict in the Middle East and weather-related crop losses could still drive up food prices and make it harder for vulnerable families to afford basic staples.

The WFP also warned that funding cuts from the United States and Europe are making it harder to track emerging hunger crises. Bauer described a growing shortage of food security data, saying the agency conducted about 1.1 million household surveys in 2024 but only around 800,000 this year because of reduced funding.





open image in gallery
A woman fetches drinking water from an unprotected well, as Zimbabwe is experiencing an El Nino-induced drought (Reuters)
"At a time when you have a risk like an El Niño, it is important to have high-frequency data collection," Bauer said, warning that weaker monitoring could delay the response to worsening food emergencies.


Current forecasts point to below-average rainfall across parts of East Africa, the Sahel, Central America and the Caribbean, while flooding risks are expected to rise in Somalia and neighboring countries. Parts of South and Southeast Asia could also face drought, disrupted monsoons and localized flooding that threaten crop production.



The WFP said it has already expanded anticipatory aid programs in 18 countries, reaching more than 1.3 million people this year with cash assistance and other support designed to lessen the impact of extreme weather before disaster strikes.

articles.summary: The UN World Food Programme has warned that a powerful El Niño weather pattern could push nearly 49 million more people into acute hunger by the end of next year, bringing the total to around 274 million across 45 vulnerable countries. There is an 81% chance of a very strong El Niño developing, with Pacific Ocean temperatures expected to reach their highest levels since at least 1982, potentially making it the strongest El Niño since 1950. Central America and Southern Africa are expected to be hardest hit, with food insecurity projected to rise by 83% and 75% respectively, driven by widespread droughts, floods and erratic rainfall threatening food production.

articles.title: New car sales surge in UK amid electric vehicle revolution
articles.jina_text:
New car registrations in the UK increased by 11.7 per cent in July, marking the eighth consecutive month of growth, with a total of 156,571 vehicles registered according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT). 
Demand for electric vehicles (EVs) was a significant driver of this growth, rising by 44.5 per cent to 43,106 cars, now accounting for 14.9 per cent of the car market, while plug-in hybrids also saw a 33.6 per cent increase. 
Conversely, registrations for diesel and petrol cars experienced declines, dropping by 5.2 per cent and 17.7 per cent respectively during the same period. 
Growth was observed across all car buying sectors, with private buyer uptake increasing by 12.6 per cent and fleet deliveries rising by 9.5 per cent, representing six in ten registrations. 
The SMMT forecasts that electric vehicles will achieve a 27.4 per cent market share by the end of the year, though chief executive Mike Hawes expressed concerns that manufacturers are facing financial strain from EV discounts, which could jeopardise future investment and viability despite the industry's commitment to decarbonisation.

articles.title: How the future of British farming is transforming due to climate change
articles.raw_rss: Heatwaves could allow farmers to consider new crops that previously ‘we could never imagine’ growing in the UK
articles.raw_meta: Heatwaves could allow farmers to consider new crops that previously ‘we could never imagine’ growing in the UK
articles.jina_text:
With drought conditions declared across half of England, British farmers are continuing to face the extreme effects of climate change. 
Amid increasing reports of reduced crop yields and predicted food shortages, growers across the country are rushing to adapt to what the Met Office has termed the “new normal”.
With several heatwaves and temperature records broken over the last few weeks, these conditions have contributed to what has been recognised as “one of the worst harvests in living memory”.





With typical British produce such as sweetcorn, green beans, garden peas, and broccoli beginning to struggle, some experts have suggested the warmer temperatures are an opportunity for Britain to diversify its fruit and vegetable production. 
Here, The Independent finds out what crops could one day be grown in the UK, potentially changing the future of farming across the country.






open image in gallery
For farmers across the country, climate change has become ‘a constant reality’ (AFP/Getty)

Fruit 
Charlie Taverner, policy lead at the Food, Farming and Countryside Commission, said: “Climate change has become a constant reality that our farmers are grappling with – they’re at the forefront of this all.


“But while we’re seeing an awful lot of apprehension, we have to see the opportunity. Some crops that we could never even imagine growing here are now becoming viable.” 
He suggested a wider variety of fruit trees, olives and grapes are starting to become more viable in the UK without the use of polytunnels.



“Things which traditionally grow in warmer, Mediterranean climates are now showing more potential to be grown here,” Mr Taverner said.

Vegetables
For vegetable growers, this summer has been particularly hard, as leafy greens, carrots and pumpkins are among those which have seen large declines in yield. 





But Liz Mooney from the Royal Horticultural Society said: “The climate is definitely having a major impact on what agriculture in the UK could look like in the future. 
“Sweet potatoes, sweet peppers, artichokes and chillies are all vegetables that are now able to grow here, without the need for greenhouses or extra equipment.”
She added even tomatoes, which usually have to be grown in temperature-controlled conditions, are now showing success when grown outside.





open image in gallery
The heat has allowed a larger variety of vegetables to be grown in the UK without extra equipment (AFP/Getty)
But she emphasised the potential of these crops is not based on warm weather alone. 
“If we want to be able to grow anything, we need to ensure we’re doing our best to protect our soil, practice sustainability, and diversify what we’re planting – if we do that, then something will always grow well,” Ms Mooney said.

Legumes
Legumes, which the UK predominantly imports from South America and Asia, are similarly showing viability for growth domestically.
